docs.title: Cell Junctions Explorer
docs.text: View Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This interactive diagram compares the four major types of cell junctions found in animal and plant tissues. The image is organized as a 2x2 grid showing tight junctions, desmosomes, gap junctions, and plasmodesmata in cross-section between adjacent cells.

Use Explore mode to hover over each structure and learn about its molecular components and biological function. Switch to Quiz mode to test your ability to identify junction components.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode — Hover over any numbered marker or label to see a description and AP exam tip
  2. Quiz mode — A structure name appears in the prompt; click the correct marker on the diagram
  3. Compare junction types by exploring structures across all four quadrants

docs.title: Junction Types at a Glance
docs.text: Junction Type Key Proteins Function Found In Tight Junction Claudins, occludins Seals intercellular space; prevents leakage Epithelial tissues (gut, kidney, bladder) Desmosome Cadherins (desmoglein), keratin Mechanical anchoring; resists stretching Skin, heart muscle, uterus Gap Junction Connexins (6 per connexon) Direct cytoplasmic communication; passes ions and second messengers Heart muscle, smooth muscle, neurons Plasmodesma Plasma membrane + desmotubule (ER) Plant cell-to-cell channel; symplastic transport All plant tissues

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: 9-12 (AP Biology)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Plasma membrane structure
  • Cytoskeleton components (intermediate filaments)
  • Cell signaling basics (second messengers)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Use Explore mode to examine all four junction types, focusing on structural proteins and their functions
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Compare tight junctions (sealing) vs. gap junctions (communication) — how do their structures reflect their opposite functions?
  3. Assessment (5 min): Complete Quiz mode; then answer: How are gap junctions and plasmodesmata analogous? How do they differ structurally?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Can students explain why tight junctions force transcellular (not paracellular) transport?
  • Can students distinguish the mechanical role of desmosomes from the sealing role of tight junctions?
  • Can students compare gap junctions (animal) to plasmodesmata (plant) as analogous structures?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Cell junction — Wikipedia
  2. Tight junction — Wikipedia
  3. Gap junction — Wikipedia
  4. Plasmodesma — Wikipedia

docs.title: Image Prompt: Cell Junctions Explorer
docs.text: CRITICAL: No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image. No figure captions, scale bars, or legends. Repeat: absolutely NO text of any kind.

docs.title: Technical Specifications
docs.text:
• Aspect ratio: landscape 4:3
  • Resolution: 1200 x 900 px
  • Style: biological textbook illustration, clean line art with light color fills, white background, AP Biology high school level
  • The image must contain NO text, labels, numbers, arrows, or annotations of any kind

docs.title: Overall Layout
docs.text:
The image is divided into four equal quadrants (2x2 grid), each showing a cross-sectional view of two adjacent cells with a different type of cell junction between them. A thin white dividing line separates the four panels.

  • Upper-left quadrant: Tight Junction (animal cells)
  • Upper-right quadrant: Desmosome (animal cells)
  • Lower-left quadrant: Gap Junction (animal cells)
  • Lower-right quadrant: Plasmodesma (plant cells)

Each quadrant shows two adjacent cells with their plasma membranes clearly visible and the junction structure at the interface between them.

docs.title: All Quadrants — Common Elements
docs.text:
• Plasma membrane — thin orange/gold (#F39C12) line forming the boundary of each cell, clearly visible in all four panels
  • Intercellular space — narrow pale gray (#BDC3C7) gap between the two cells
  • Cell cytoplasm — pale warm beige (#F5F0E8) fill inside each cell
  • Each cell should occupy roughly half the quadrant width, meeting in the center

docs.title: Upper-Left: Tight Junction
docs.text:
• Two rectangular epithelial cells side by side with clear apical (top) and basal (bottom) orientation
  • Tight junction seal — bright red (#E74C3C) band running horizontally across the intercellular space near the apical surface, shown as multiple interlocking protein strands
  • Claudin/occludin proteins — dark red (#C0392B) paired transmembrane stalks that cross from one cell's membrane to the other, forming the interlocking seal. Show 4-5 pairs of these interlocking proteins
  • The intercellular space should be visibly sealed (closed) above the tight junction and visibly open below it
  • Must have at least 40 px of clear space at the junction site for a callout marker

docs.title: Upper-Right: Desmosome
docs.text:
• Two adjacent cells with a disc-shaped junction between them
  • Dense cytoplasmic plaques — thick purple (#8E44AD) rectangular bars on the inner surface of each cell's membrane at the junction site
  • Cadherin proteins (desmoglein/desmocollin) — medium purple (#9B59B6) paired stalk proteins spanning the intercellular space, connecting the two plaques. Show 5-6 pairs
  • Intermediate filaments — dark purple (#7D3C98) thick wavy lines looping through each plaque and extending deep into the cytoplasm of each cell. Show bundles of 3-4 filaments on each side
  • The desmosome should look like a symmetric disc or button connecting the two cells

docs.title: Lower-Left: Gap Junction
docs.text:
• Two adjacent cells with a cluster of cylindrical channels between them
  • Connexon hemichannels — blue (#2980B9) cylindrical structures, each spanning one cell's membrane. Show 3-4 complete gap junction channels (each = two connexons docked end-to-end)
  • Connexin subunits — show one connexon in cross-section view (ring of six dark blue (#2471A3) subunits around a central pore) alongside the longitudinal view
  • Small passing molecules — light blue (#5DADE2) small circles/dots shown passing through the channels from one cell to the other, representing ions and second messengers
  • The gap between the two cells should be very narrow (~2-4 nm implied) at the junction site

docs.title: Lower-Right: Plasmodesma
docs.text:
• Two adjacent plant cells with thick cellulose cell walls
  • Cell walls — thick bright green (#2ECC71) layers on the outer surface of each cell, much thicker than the plasma membrane
  • Plasmodesma channel — a narrow passage through the cell wall, lined by continuous plasma membrane (orange), connecting the two cells' cytoplasm
  • Desmotubule — dark green (#1E8449) thin strand running through the center of the plasmodesma channel, representing compressed ER
  • Annular space — narrow pale region between the desmotubule and the outer membrane lining, where molecules pass
  • Show 2-3 plasmodesmata channels through the wall to indicate they occur in clusters

docs.title: Spatial Relationships
docs.text:
• All four panels should be at roughly the same magnification/scale
  • The junction structures should be prominently centered in each quadrant
  • Each structure must have enough visual space (30-40 px minimum) for a callout marker dot
  • The two cells in each panel should be clearly distinguishable with their membranes visible
  • Colors must be distinct enough between quadrants to immediately identify which junction type is which

docs.title: What NOT to Include
docs.text:
• No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, or annotations of any kind
  • No figure captions or scale bars
  • No gradient fills that obscure structure boundaries
  • No artistic flourishes, bokeh, or photorealistic lighting
  • No decorative backgrounds

CRITICAL: No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image.

docs.title: Cell Membrane — Fluid Mosaic Model
docs.text:
View Fullscreen

The fluid mosaic model describes the plasma membrane as a dynamic, two-dimensional fluid in which a mosaic of proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates can move laterally. The 13 structures shown in the diagram are central to AP Biology Unit 2 (Cell Structure and Function).

docs.title: Phospholipid Bilayer
docs.text: Two back-to-back sheets of phospholipids with hydrophilic heads facing the aqueous environments on each side and hydrophobic tails forming the waterproof interior core. This arrangement is the basis of selective permeability.

docs.title: Hydrophilic Head
docs.text: The polar, charged head group of each phospholipid — a glycerol-phosphate unit that is attracted to water and faces outward on both membrane surfaces.

docs.title: Hydrophobic Tail
docs.text: The two nonpolar fatty-acid chains that extend inward. Saturation affects their packing: saturated tails pack tightly (less fluid); unsaturated tails with kinks stay more loosely packed (more fluid).

docs.title: Integral Protein
docs.text: Permanently embedded in the bilayer, spanning one or both leaflets. The portions within the hydrophobic core have nonpolar side chains; the portions exposed to aqueous environments have polar or charged side chains.

docs.title: Peripheral Protein
docs.text: Loosely associated with the membrane surface — attached to head groups or integral proteins but not embedded in the hydrophobic core. Removable without detergents. Functions include signal relay and cytoskeleton anchoring.

docs.title: Channel Protein
docs.text: A transmembrane protein with a hydrophilic pore allowing specific ions or small polar molecules to cross by facilitated diffusion — no ATP required, movement is down the concentration gradient. Aquaporins are a key example.

docs.title: Carrier Protein
docs.text: A transmembrane protein that binds a solute, changes conformation, and releases it on the other side. Works by facilitated diffusion (passive) or active transport (requires ATP). Unlike channels, it does not form an open pore.

docs.title: Receptor Protein
docs.text: A transmembrane protein with an extracellular binding domain that recognizes a specific ligand (hormone, neurotransmitter, etc.). Ligand binding triggers an intracellular signal transduction cascade — the signal does not enter the cell.

docs.title: Cholesterol
docs.text: A steroid lipid wedged between phospholipids in animal cell membranes. Acts as a fluidity buffer — reducing excess fluidity at high temperatures and preventing solidification at low temperatures.

docs.title: Glycoprotein
docs.text: An integral protein with branching oligosaccharide chains on the extracellular face. Part of the glycocalyx; critical for cell-cell recognition and immune response. ABO blood group antigens are glycoproteins.

docs.title: Glycolipid
docs.text: A phospholipid in the outer leaflet with a short sugar chain on its extracellular head. Contributes to the glycocalyx and cell surface identity.

docs.title: Extracellular Space
docs.text: The aqueous environment outside the cell, where signaling molecules arrive and where extracellular concentration gradients drive diffusion and osmosis across the membrane.

docs.title: Intracellular Space
docs.text: The cytoplasm side of the membrane, where signal transduction cascades are initiated, where active transport pumps hydrolyze ATP, and where peripheral proteins anchor the cytoskeleton to the bilayer.

docs.title: Chemical Equation Rendering Pipeline
docs.text: Open Full Screen

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This diagram traces the complete pipeline that transforms $\ce{H2O}$ written in a generated markdown file into a beautifully typeset chemical formula in the browser. The pipeline begins with CLAUDE.md — the project rulebook that instructs the chapter-content-generator skill to use dollar notation exclusively — and then passes through five processing layers: Python extension, build, browser loading, and MathJax rendering.

Hover over each node to read a detailed explanation of that step.

docs.title: Pipeline Steps
docs.text:
1. CLAUDE.md prerequisite — Must specify the dollar notation rule; instructs the content generator to never use backslash notation
  2. chapter-content-generator skill — Reads CLAUDE.md and generates .md content using $...$ and $\ce{...}$
  3. arithmatex intercepts — pymdownx.arithmatex captures $ delimiters before Python-Markdown runs
  4. Protected spans — Math content is wrapped in <span class="arithmatex"> and converted to \(...\) internally
  5. Python-Markdown runs — Processes headings, links, lists with math content safely isolated
  6. MkDocs assembles — Builds the full HTML page with all CSS and JS references
  7. Browser loads — Page loads with equations as unrendered protected spans
  8. mathjax-config.js — Declares the mhchem package and sets delimiters; must load before the CDN bundle
  9. MathJax CDN — Full tex-chtml.js bundle loads (full bundle required for mhchem)
  10. DOM scan — MathJax finds all \(...\) and \[...\] spans queued for typesetting
  11. mhchem extension — Processes \ce{...} into proper chemical notation with subscripts, arrows, and charges
  12. Rendered output — Final typeset equations and chemical formulas appear to the reader

docs.title: Key Design Decision
docs.text:
The pymdownx.arithmatex extension (with generic: true) acts as a protective shield. By intercepting $ delimiters before Python-Markdown processes the document, it prevents the Markdown parser from misinterpreting chemical formulas that contain [] or () — which look identical to Markdown link syntax.

The rule: Always write $ and $$ in markdown. Never write \(...\) or \[...\] directly in .md files.

This rule must be encoded in CLAUDE.md so the chapter-content-generator skill enforces it automatically. Without the explicit instruction in CLAUDE.md, an AI content generator defaults to backslash notation, which breaks the pipeline.

docs.title: Chi-Square Test Calculator
docs.text: View Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text: This calculator walks students through every computational stage of the chi-square (χ²) statistical test — the primary tool AP Biology uses to evaluate whether observed genetic cross results match Mendelian expected ratios. Students enter their own observed counts, choose an expected ratio (3:1, 1:2:1, or 9:3:3:1), and watch the step-by-step table populate with O, E, (O−E), (O−E)², and (O−E)²/E values before revealing the χ² total, critical value comparison, and a color-coded accept/reject verdict.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Choose an expected ratio from the dropdown (default: 3:1 monohybrid dominant).
  2. Enter observed counts in the blue input cells — expected counts update automatically.
  3. Click Calculate χ² to reveal the full step-by-step calculation and decision.
  4. Check Show worked explanation for a plain-language narrative of the result.
  5. Click Reset to restore the default values and try a new scenario.
  6. Switch ratios (1:2:1 or 9:3:3:1) to practice dihybrid and codominant crosses.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text: Term Meaning Observed (O) The actual counts from your experiment Expected (E) Counts predicted by the Mendelian ratio, scaled to your sample size (O − E)² / E Each category's contribution to the χ² statistic χ² statistic Sum of all (O − E)² / E values Degrees of freedom (df) Number of categories minus one Critical value The χ² threshold at p = 0.05; exceeding it → reject null hypothesis

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text:
<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/biology/sims/chi-square-calculator/main.html"
        height="560"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: 9–12 (AP Biology, Unit 1 and Unit 5)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 20–30 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Understanding of Mendelian inheritance and phenotypic ratios
  • Familiarity with mean and basic descriptive statistics
  • Ability to read and interpret a simple data table

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Students will calculate the chi-square statistic from observed and expected genetic cross data, compare the result to a critical value table, and determine whether to reject the null hypothesis.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Launch (3 min): Open the calculator with default values (290 dominant, 110 recessive, 3:1 ratio). Before clicking Calculate, ask students: "Do these numbers look close to the expected 300:100 split? How would you decide if the difference is 'too big' to be chance?"

  2. Guided walkthrough — 3:1 (7 min): Click Calculate χ² together. Walk through each column in the step-by-step table, pausing at (O−E)²/E to discuss why we square the difference. Point out the highlighted row in the critical value table. Read the verdict aloud.

  3. Student practice — modify values (5 min): Have students change the observed counts to something clearly non-Mendelian (e.g., 350 dominant, 50 recessive) and recalculate. Ask: "What changed? Why did the verdict flip?"

  4. Switch to 9:3:3:1 (7 min): Select the dihybrid ratio. Discuss why df increases to 3 and why the critical value rises to 7.82. Have students enter realistic dihybrid counts and interpret the result.

  5. Worked explanation (3 min): Check the "Show worked explanation" box. Have students compare the narrative to their own interpretation. Discuss what "fail to reject the null hypothesis" means — it does not mean the hypothesis is proven true.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Given a table of observed dihybrid cross results, students calculate χ² by hand and verify using the sim.
  • Explain in one sentence why a large χ² value leads to rejecting the null hypothesis.
  • Describe what degrees of freedom represents in a chi-square test.
  • Predict whether changing the sample size (N) while keeping the same proportions will change the χ² value, and test the prediction using the calculator.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Fail to reject = accept the hypothesis" — failure to reject only means the data are consistent with the null; it does not prove Mendelian ratios.
  • "Bigger sample always gives the same χ²" — doubling N while keeping proportions constant doubles χ², making it easier to detect real deviations.
  • "df = number of categories" — degrees of freedom is categories minus one.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chi-Squared Test — Wikipedia
  2. Mendelian Inheritance — Wikipedia
  3. AP Biology Course and Exam Description — College Board

docs.title: Chloroplast & Light Reactions (Thylakoid Membrane)
docs.text:
View Fullscreen

This interactive diagram covers 16 structures of the chloroplast and the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis (AP Biology Unit 3). The upper section shows the overall chloroplast architecture; the lower zoom reveals the four protein complexes of the thylakoid electron transport chain in the order electrons flow: PSII → Cyt b6f → PSI → ATP synthase.

docs.title: Outer Membrane
docs.text: The smooth, freely permeable outer boundary of the chloroplast envelope. Porins allow small molecules (up to ~10 kDa) to pass without active transport. Does not control selective metabolite exchange — that role belongs to the inner membrane.

docs.title: Inner Membrane
docs.text: The selectively permeable inner layer of the chloroplast envelope. Transporter proteins — especially the triose phosphate/phosphate translocator — regulate the export of Calvin cycle products (G3P) to the cytoplasm and the import of inorganic phosphate. Not the site of the light reactions.

docs.title: Stroma
docs.text: The aqueous fluid inside the chloroplast (enclosed by the inner membrane). Site of the Calvin cycle (carbon fixation, reduction, RuBP regeneration). Receives ATP and NADPH from the thylakoid membrane and releases G3P. Contains chloroplast DNA, ribosomes, and Calvin cycle enzymes including RuBisCO.

docs.title: Granum (Thylakoid Stack)
docs.text: A stack of 5–20 flattened thylakoid discs interconnected by stroma lamellae. Stacking increases membrane surface area for light-harvesting complexes. A single chloroplast contains 10–100 grana.

docs.title: Thylakoid Membrane
docs.text: The inner membrane system where all four light-reaction protein complexes are embedded. Creates a sealed lumen compartment that accumulates H⁺, driving ATP synthesis. Analogous to the inner mitochondrial membrane.

docs.title: Thylakoid Lumen
docs.text: The aqueous interior space enclosed by the thylakoid membrane. Receives H⁺ from water splitting (at PSII) and from plastoquinol oxidation (at Cyt b6f), becoming acidic (pH ~5) during illumination. This H⁺ reservoir powers CF₁ ATP synthase.

docs.title: Photosystem II (PSII)
docs.text: P680 — the first complex in linear electron flow. Absorbs photons, uses the energy to oxidize water (\(\ce{2H2O -> O2 + 4H+ + 4e-}\)), and passes electrons to plastoquinone. The oxygen-evolving complex on the lumenal face coordinates a Mn₄CaO₅ cluster to accomplish water splitting.

docs.title: H₂O → O₂ (Water Splitting)
docs.text: Photolysis of water at the oxygen-evolving complex of PSII. Two water molecules yield one O₂ molecule, four H⁺ ions (released into the lumen), and four electrons (passed to P680). All atmospheric O₂ on Earth originates from this reaction.

docs.title: Plastoquinone (PQ)
docs.text: A small, hydrophobic mobile carrier embedded in the thylakoid membrane lipid bilayer. Accepts 2e⁻ and 2H⁺ from PSII to become plastoquinol (PQH₂), diffuses laterally to the cytochrome b6f complex, and releases its H⁺ into the lumen — directly contributing to the proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis.

docs.title: Cytochrome b6f Complex
docs.text: The central "hub" of the light reactions — analogous to Complex III of the mitochondrial ETC. Oxidizes plastoquinol, pumps additional H⁺ into the lumen via the Q-cycle, and reduces plastocyanin. The rate-limiting step of linear electron flow. Also the branching point for cyclic electron flow.

docs.title: Plastocyanin (PC)
docs.text: A small, copper-containing soluble protein in the thylakoid lumen. Shuttles one electron at a time from the cytochrome b6f complex to the P700⁺ reaction center of PSI. Its copper alternates between Cu⁺ (reduced) and Cu²⁺ (oxidized) with each electron transfer.

docs.title: Photosystem I (PSI)
docs.text: P700 — the second light-driven reaction center. Re-energizes electrons received from plastocyanin and passes them via ferredoxin to FNR, which reduces \(\ce{NADP+ + H+ + 2e- -> NADPH}\). PSI is also the site of cyclic electron flow, which produces additional ATP without NADPH or O₂.

docs.title: Ferredoxin (Fd)
docs.text: A small, soluble iron-sulfur protein on the stromal face of PSI. Accepts high-energy electrons from P700 one at a time and delivers them to FNR (ferredoxin-NADP⁺ reductase) for NADPH synthesis. Also donates electrons to the cytochrome b6f complex during cyclic electron flow.

docs.title: NADP⁺ / NADPH
docs.text: The terminal electron acceptor of the light reactions. FNR pairs two single-electron transfers from ferredoxin to reduce one NADP⁺ to NADPH. NADPH is consumed in the Calvin cycle to reduce 3-PGA to G3P via the enzyme GAPDH. It is analogous to NADH in cellular respiration but carries electrons at a higher energy state.

docs.title: ATP Synthase (CF₁)
docs.text: Chloroplast ATP synthase (CF₀CF₁) uses H⁺ flow from lumen to stroma to phosphorylate ADP + Pᵢ → ATP in the stroma. The CF₀ transmembrane domain forms the H⁺ channel; the CF₁ catalytic head protrudes into the stroma. Rotation of the central γ-subunit drives conformational changes in the three catalytic β-subunits, each cycling through open, loose, and tight conformations (binding change mechanism).

docs.title: Proton Gradient (H⁺ Flow)
docs.text: The proton-motive force across the thylakoid membrane is the driving force for photophosphorylation. H⁺ accumulates in the lumen from three sources: water splitting at PSII, the Q-cycle at cytochrome b6f, and H⁺ consumption in the stroma by NADPH synthesis and Calvin cycle reactions. The resulting ΔpH (~3 units) provides the energy for ATP synthase to produce ATP from ADP + Pᵢ.

docs.text: Run the Comparative Anatomy Explorer Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text: This interactive explorer displays the forelimbs of five vertebrate species — human, whale, bat, dog, and bird — side by side with color-coded skeletal overlays. The same five bone groups (humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, phalanges) appear in each species, modified by natural selection for different functions. This is one of the strongest lines of evidence for common ancestry.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore Mode: Hover over any bone in any species to highlight the same bone across all five species simultaneously. An info box describes the bone's adaptation in that species.
  2. Toggle Bones: Click "Hide Bones" to see just the silhouettes, then reveal bones again.
  3. Quiz Mode: Click "Switch to Quiz Mode" to test your knowledge. You'll be presented with pairs of structures to classify as homologous, analogous, or vestigial. Immediate feedback explains the reasoning.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: 9-12 (AP Biology)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Basic understanding of natural selection and common ancestry.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Students hover over each bone type across all five species. Ask: "What stays the same? What changes? Why?"
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Discuss the difference between homologous structures (same origin, different function) and analogous structures (different origin, same function). Use the bone legend to trace each bone across species.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Switch to Quiz Mode. Students classify 8 structure pairs and review feedback.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Students can correctly identify homologous, analogous, and vestigial structures.
  • Students can explain why shared bone structure across species is evidence for common descent.
  • Students score at least 6/8 on the classification quiz.

docs.title: Comparative Anatomy — Forelimb Homology Image Prompt
Comparative Anatomy — Forelimb Homology Image Prompt
Purpose
docs.text: Generate a single wide illustration showing the forelimbs of five vertebrate species side by side. The image will be used as a background for an interactive MicroSim where students hover over bones to learn about homologous structures. No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image.

docs.title: Global Specifications
docs.text:
• Aspect ratio: 5:2 landscape (1500 × 600 px)
  • Style: Clean biological textbook illustration, precise anatomical line art with flat color fills, white background, AP Biology high school level
  • Layout: Five equal-width vertical panels arranged horizontally, separated by thin light-gray divider lines. Each panel contains one species forelimb.
  • Orientation: All forelimbs oriented vertically with the shoulder/proximal end at the top and digits/distal end at the bottom
  • Background: Pure white within each panel
  • No text of any kind in the image. No labels, no species names, no bone names, no numbers, no arrows, no annotation marks. Repeat: absolutely no text.

docs.title: Bone Color Code (consistent across all five species)
docs.text:
Bone Group Color Hex Humerus Red #E74C3C Radius Medium blue #3498DB Ulna Dark blue #2471A3 Carpals Green #27AE60 Metacarpals & Phalanges Yellow #F1C40F

Each bone must be filled with its assigned color at full opacity with a thin dark outline (1-2px, dark gray #333). Adjacent bones of different colors must have a visible gap or distinct outline so they never blend together.

docs.title: Panel 1 — Human Arm (leftmost)
docs.text:
Draw a human right arm from shoulder to fingertips, anterior (palm-forward) view, showing internal skeletal structure through a semi-transparent flesh silhouette.

  • Flesh silhouette: Very light peach/skin tone (#FDEBD0), 15% opacity outline of the full arm shape — muscular upper arm tapering to a narrower forearm, widening slightly at the wrist, then five distinct spread fingers
  • Humerus (red): Single long bone running from the top of the panel down to the elbow region, roughly 35% of the total limb length. Slightly wider at the proximal (shoulder) end, narrowing at the shaft, widening again at the distal (elbow) end with visible condyles
  • Radius (medium blue): On the lateral (thumb) side of the forearm. Narrower at the elbow, wider at the wrist. Runs from elbow to wrist, about 30% of limb length
  • Ulna (dark blue): On the medial (pinky) side. Prominent olecranon process (elbow point) at the top. Wider at the elbow, tapering toward the wrist. Slightly longer than the radius
  • Carpals (green): Cluster of 8 small irregular rounded bones at the wrist, arranged in two rows of four. Each carpal bone individually outlined
  • Phalanges (yellow): Five metacarpals fanning out from the carpals, each leading to 3 phalanges (2 for the thumb). The fingers are spread apart, clearly showing all 14 phalanges as individual bone segments connected at visible joints. The thumb is shorter and offset

Key visual: Long, straight proportions. Fingers long and separated. This is the "generalized" mammalian forelimb plan.

docs.title: Panel 2 — Whale Flipper
docs.text:
Draw a right whale flipper in lateral view, showing internal skeletal structure through a semi-transparent flipper silhouette.

  • Flipper silhouette: Light blue-gray (#D6EAF8), smooth paddle shape — narrow at the shoulder, broadening dramatically into a wide, rounded paddle with no visible finger separation on the exterior
  • Humerus (red): Extremely short and thick — almost a squat rectangle. Only about 10-12% of the total flipper length. Very wide relative to its length. Positioned at the very top of the flipper
  • Radius (medium blue): Short and flattened into a wide disc-like shape. Positioned side by side with the ulna below the humerus
  • Ulna (dark blue): Similar short, wide, flattened shape as the radius. Together they look like two wide plates rather than long rods
  • Carpals (green): Small rounded bones clustered in a compact group below radius/ulna. Fewer and more reduced than in the human
  • Phalanges (yellow): This is where the whale flipper is dramatically different — the metacarpals and phalanges are greatly elongated and numerous (hyperphalangy). Show 5 rays of many small yellow bone segments fanning out and filling the entire broad paddle area. The individual phalanges are small rectangular segments stacked in long chains. They occupy about 60-65% of the total flipper length. The rays spread widely to fill the paddle shape

Key visual: Tiny humerus, tiny radius/ulna, but enormously elongated phalanges filling a broad paddle. The bones are embedded inside a smooth, teardrop paddle shape.

docs.title: Panel 3 — Bat Wing
docs.text:
Draw a right bat wing from shoulder to wingtip, dorsal view with the wing partially extended, showing internal skeletal structure through a semi-transparent wing membrane.

  • Wing membrane (patagium): Very light purple (#F5EEF8), thin translucent membrane stretching between the elongated fingers. The membrane extends from the body (left edge) out to the fingertips and down to where the leg would be
  • Humerus (red): Short and robust, about 15% of total wing length. Thick bone angled slightly outward from the body
  • Radius (medium blue): Long and thin — much longer than the humerus. About 25% of wing span. This is the dominant forearm bone in bats
  • Ulna (dark blue): Very reduced and thin, running parallel to but much shorter than the radius. Barely visible — just a thin sliver alongside the radius
  • Carpals (green): Small cluster of bones at the wrist joint where the wing "bends"
  • Phalanges (yellow): This is the most dramatic feature — four enormously elongated finger rays (digits 2-5) spread out like umbrella spokes supporting the wing membrane. Each finger has 2-3 very long, thin phalanges. The longest finger (digit 3) extends to the wingtip and is about 50% of the total wing length. Show the fingers spread apart with the translucent membrane visible between them. One short thumb with a claw visible at the wrist bend (not part of the wing membrane)

Key visual: Short humerus, long radius, vestigial ulna, and spectacularly elongated finger bones spreading apart like tent poles supporting the membrane. The wing shape is clearly visible.

docs.title: Panel 4 — Dog Forelimb
docs.text:
Draw a right dog (medium-sized breed like a Labrador) forelimb from shoulder to paw, lateral view, showing internal skeletal structure through a semi-transparent leg silhouette.

  • Leg silhouette: Light tan/buff (#FAE5D3), muscular at the shoulder tapering to a slender lower leg, ending in a compact paw with visible toe pads
  • Humerus (red): Long and robust with prominent muscle attachment ridges (deltoid tuberosity visible as a bump). About 30% of limb length. Angled slightly backward from vertical
  • Radius (medium blue): Straight and strong, weight-bearing. Runs from elbow to wrist, about 28% of limb length. The radius is the primary weight-bearing forearm bone
  • Ulna (dark blue): Runs parallel to the radius with a prominent olecranon (elbow point) projecting upward behind the humerus. Slightly thinner than the radius but similar length
  • Carpals (green): Compact cluster of small bones. The dog "wrist" is what most people think is the dog's "knee" on the front leg — positioned high above the paw
  • Phalanges (yellow): Short and compact. Four main toes (digits 2-5) with a small dewclaw (digit 1) higher up. Each toe has 3 short phalanges. The dog walks on its toes (digitigrade), so the metacarpals are elongated and nearly vertical, with the phalanges angled to meet the ground. Show small claw shapes at the tips

Key visual: Proportionally similar to human but with the limb adapted for running — the "wrist" is high up, the animal walks on its toes, and the bones are robust for weight bearing.

docs.title: Panel 5 — Bird Wing (rightmost)
docs.text:
Draw a right bird wing (eagle or hawk) partially extended, dorsal view, showing internal skeletal structure through a semi-transparent wing silhouette with feather outlines.

  • Wing silhouette: Very light green (#EAFAF1), elongated airfoil shape with visible feather outlines along the trailing edge — long primary flight feathers at the tip, shorter secondary feathers along the inner wing
  • Humerus (red): Short, thick, and hollow-looking (show it slightly lighter/translucent to suggest pneumatic bone). About 20% of wing length. Held close to the body
  • Radius (medium blue): Long and thin, running from elbow to wrist. About 30% of wing length
  • Ulna (dark blue): Slightly thicker than the radius and curved. The secondary flight feathers attach along the ulna. Show small bumps (quill knobs) along the ulna where feather shafts anchor
  • Carpals (green): Greatly reduced — only two small bones visible at the wrist. These are fused in birds (carpometacarpus), so show them as a compact unit
  • Phalanges (yellow): Dramatically reduced and fused. Only three digits remain, and they are mostly fused into a single pointed structure (the alula digit is separate and small). Show the fused metacarpals and reduced phalanges as a single tapering yellow structure at the wingtip. The primary flight feathers attach here. This is strikingly different from the bat — instead of long separate fingers, the bird has a rigid fused hand

Key visual: Hollow humerus, prominent ulna with feather attachments, and a fused/reduced hand — the opposite strategy from the bat. The wing is rigid and feathered rather than flexible and membranous.

docs.title: Composition Notes
docs.text:
• All five limbs should be drawn at approximately the same total height within their panels so they can be visually compared
  • The shoulder/proximal end should align horizontally across all five panels
  • Each limb should be centered horizontally within its panel
  • Leave enough white space around each limb for overlay markers (at least 15% padding on each side)
  • The color fills must be flat and solid — no gradients, no shading, no drop shadows on the bones
  • The semi-transparent flesh/membrane silhouettes should be just visible enough to show the overall limb shape without obscuring the bone colors
  • Bone outlines should be clean, 1-2px dark gray lines with no sketchy or hand-drawn effect

No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image. This is critical — the interactive overlay adds all labels programmatically.

docs.title: Condensation and Hydrolysis Reaction Simulator
docs.text: Run the Condensation and Hydrolysis Reaction Simulator Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This simulation demonstrates the two fundamental reactions that build and break biological polymers:

  • Condensation (dehydration synthesis) — two monomers join together, releasing a water molecule (\(\ce{H2O}\)). The \(\ce{-OH}\) group from one monomer and the \(\ce{H-}\) from the other combine to form water. This reaction requires energy input.

  • Hydrolysis — a water molecule splits and its components (\(\ce{-OH}\) and \(\ce{H-}\)) reattach to the broken bond ends, freeing a monomer. This reaction releases energy.

Students can observe these reactions across three polymer types: polypeptides (amino acids), polysaccharides (glucose units), and polynucleotides (nucleotides).

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Select a reaction type from the dropdown: Polypeptide, Polysaccharide, or Polynucleotide
  2. Click "Add Monomer" to watch a condensation reaction — observe the red-highlighted atoms that leave to form water
  3. Click "Hydrolyze" to break the last bond — watch water split and reattach to the freed monomers
  4. Click "Build to 5" to rapidly build a short polymer chain
  5. Watch the energy indicator (upper right) to see whether energy is required or released
  6. Track the water counter to see how many water molecules have been released

docs.title: Key Observations
docs.text:
• Each condensation reaction removes one \(\ce{H2O}\) and requires energy
  • Each hydrolysis reaction consumes one \(\ce{H2O}\) and releases energy
  • The number of bonds is always one less than the number of monomers
  • The same \(\ce{-OH}\) and \(\ce{H-}\) pattern applies to all three polymer types

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: 9-12 (AP Biology)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Understanding of atoms and chemical bonds
  • Familiarity with the concept of monomers and polymers

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Students select each reaction type and perform 3-4 condensation reactions, observing which atoms leave to form water.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Students hydrolyze the chain back to individual monomers, noting the energy direction change and water consumption.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Students answer: "Why is condensation also called dehydration synthesis?" and "Where does the water molecule come from during condensation?"

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Students can identify which atoms (\(\ce{-OH}\) and \(\ce{H-}\)) leave to form water
  • Students can explain why condensation requires energy and hydrolysis releases energy
  • Students can predict how many water molecules are produced when building a 6-monomer chain

docs.title: Cytoskeleton Component Explorer
docs.text: View Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text: This interactive diagram compares the three major cytoskeletal filament types side by side: microfilaments (actin), microtubules (tubulin), and intermediate filaments (keratin, lamin, etc.). All 15 labeled structures include subunit composition, cross-section views, and motor proteins.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore mode: Hover over any numbered marker or label to see a description of that structure, its function, and AP exam tips.
  • Quiz mode: Click the Quiz button to test your knowledge. Labels are hidden — click the correct marker when prompted.
  • Edit mode: Open main.html?edit=true to calibrate marker positions by dragging.

docs.title: Microfilaments (Actin) — ~7 nm
docs.text:
1. Actin filament (F-actin) — Double helix of G-actin monomers
  2. G-actin monomer — Globular subunit, binds ATP
  3. Plus end — Fast-growing barbed end
  4. Minus end — Slow-growing pointed end
  5. Cross-section — Two-strand profile, thinnest filament

docs.title: Microtubules — ~25 nm
docs.text:
1. Microtubule — Hollow cylinder of 13 protofilaments
  2. Alpha-tubulin — Orange subunit, binds GTP (non-exchangeable)
  3. Beta-tubulin — Blue subunit, binds GTP (hydrolyzable)
  4. Cross-section — Ring of 13 protofilaments, hollow lumen
  5. Kinesin — Plus-end motor, anterograde transport
  6. Dynein — Minus-end motor, retrograde transport

docs.title: Intermediate Filaments — ~10 nm
docs.text:
1. Intermediate filament — Rope-like, non-polar, tensile strength
  2. Coiled-coil dimer — Two alpha-helices wound together
  3. Cross-section — Dense solid core, no lumen
  4. Keratin filaments — Epithelial cell network, connects to desmosomes

docs.title: Size Comparison
docs.text: Filament Type Diameter Monomer Polarity Motor Proteins Microfilament ~7 nm G-actin (ATP) Yes (+/−) Myosin Microtubule ~25 nm α/β-tubulin (GTP) Yes (+/−) Kinesin, Dynein Intermediate filament ~10 nm Varies (keratin, lamin, etc.) No None

docs.title: Critical Rules
docs.text: No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image.

docs.title: Image Specifications
docs.text:
• Aspect ratio: landscape 4:3
  • Resolution: 1200 × 900 px
  • Style: biological textbook illustration, clean line art with light color fills, white background, AP Biology high school level
  • Background: clean white, no decorative elements

docs.title: Subject
docs.text: A comparative illustration showing the three major cytoskeletal filament types side by side. The image is divided into three vertical panels (left, center, right) each showing one filament type. Each panel shows both a longitudinal (side) view and a cross-section view of the filament, with protein subunits clearly visible. Motor proteins and associated structures are included where relevant.

docs.title: Left Panel (~33%): Microfilaments (Actin Filaments)
docs.text:
• Actin filament (longitudinal) — Two intertwined helical strands of spherical G-actin monomers forming an F-actin double helix; color: #5DADE2 (light blue). Individual spherical monomers clearly visible along both strands. The helix should be oriented vertically with the plus end at the top and the minus end at the bottom. At least 12-14 monomers visible per strand.

  • G-actin monomer — Individual spherical subunit clearly distinguishable within the helix; color: #3498DB (medium blue). Each monomer should be a distinct sphere, ~20 px diameter.

  • Plus end — The faster-growing end of the filament at the top; slightly more spread/open appearance; color: #2ECC71 (green tint). Visually distinct from the minus end.

  • Minus end — The slower-growing end at the bottom; slightly more compact; color: #E74C3C (red tint). Visually distinct from the plus end.

  • Cross-section inset — Small circular cross-section view in the lower-left corner of this panel showing the two-strand arrangement viewed end-on; color: #5DADE2. Diameter ~7 nm implied by the thin profile.

docs.title: Center Panel (~33%): Microtubules
docs.text:
• Microtubule (longitudinal) — Hollow cylindrical tube made of 13 protofilaments, each composed of alternating alpha-tubulin and beta-tubulin heterodimers stacked vertically; oriented vertically with plus end at top, minus end at bottom. The hollow lumen should be visible. Color: alpha-tubulin #F39C12 (orange), beta-tubulin #2C3E80 (dark blue).

  • Alpha-tubulin subunit — Spherical orange subunit in the heterodimer pair; color: #F39C12. Alternates with beta-tubulin along each protofilament.

  • Beta-tubulin subunit — Spherical dark blue subunit in the heterodimer pair; color: #2C3E80. Alternates with alpha-tubulin.

  • Cross-section inset — Circular cross-section in the lower portion showing the ring of 13 protofilaments surrounding a hollow center (lumen); color: alternating #F39C12 and #2C3E80. The hollow center should be clearly visible as white/empty space. Diameter ~25 nm implied.

  • Kinesin motor protein — Small two-headed walking figure on the surface of the microtubule, positioned near the top (plus end), with two globular heads and a coiled tail carrying a small cargo vesicle; color: #27AE60 (green).

  • Dynein motor protein — Similar two-headed walking figure on the surface near the bottom (minus end), walking in the opposite direction from kinesin, also carrying cargo; color: #8E44AD (purple).

docs.title: Right Panel (~33%): Intermediate Filaments
docs.text:
• Intermediate filament (longitudinal) — Rope-like twisted bundle of fibrous protein strands; multiple coiled-coil dimers wound together into a thick rope structure; oriented vertically; color: #E67E22 (warm orange). No distinct plus/minus ends (non-polar).

  • Coiled-coil dimer — Two alpha-helical protein chains wound around each other, visible at the top where the rope partially unravels to show substructure; color: #D35400 (darker orange).

  • Tetramer — Four coiled-coil strands forming a staggered assembly, visible in a partially unwound section; color: #E67E22 and #D35400 alternating.

  • Cross-section inset — Circular cross-section showing the dense, solid core (no hollow lumen, unlike microtubules); color: #E67E22. Diameter ~10 nm implied.

  • Keratin filaments — A small cluster of intermediate filaments shown at the bottom-right, suggesting the dense network found in epithelial cells; color: #F0B27A (light orange).

docs.title: Spatial Layout Requirements
docs.text:
• Three panels of equal width, separated by subtle white space (no dividing lines)
  • Each filament oriented vertically, centered in its panel
  • Cross-section insets positioned in the lower portion of each panel
  • Motor proteins (kinesin, dynein) positioned on the microtubule surface
  • All three filaments at roughly the same vertical position for easy size comparison
  • The relative thicknesses should be approximately correct: microfilaments thinnest, intermediate filaments medium, microtubules thickest

docs.title: What NOT to Include
docs.text:
• No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image
  • No figure captions, scale bars, or legends
  • No gradient fills that blur structure boundaries
  • No artistic flourishes, bokeh, or photorealistic lighting
  • No cell membrane, nucleus, or other organelles — focus only on the three filament types

REPEAT: No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image.

docs.title: DNA Double Helix Structure
docs.text:
View Fullscreen

The DNA double helix is the molecular basis of heredity. Its structure — discovered by Watson and Crick in 1953 using X-ray diffraction data from Franklin and Wilkins — explains how genetic information is stored, copied, and expressed. The 13 structures shown are central to AP Biology Units 3 and 6 (Gene Expression and Genetics).

docs.title: Sugar-Phosphate Backbone
docs.text: The outer rails of the twisted-ladder structure — alternating deoxyribose sugars and phosphate groups linked by covalent phosphodiester bonds. Two antiparallel backbones spiral around each other; the backbones are hydrophilic and face the aqueous environment.

docs.title: Deoxyribose Sugar
docs.text: A 5-carbon pentose sugar at the core of each nucleotide. Deoxyribose lacks the 2′-hydroxyl group present in ribose (RNA's sugar), making DNA more chemically stable. Each sugar connects to one phosphate group and one nitrogenous base.

docs.title: Phosphate Group
docs.text: A negatively charged phosphate ion (\(\ce{PO4^3-}\)) that bridges adjacent sugars via phosphodiester bonds. The negative charge gives the DNA backbone its overall negative charge, enabling binding to positively charged histone proteins and migration toward the positive pole in gel electrophoresis.

docs.title: Nitrogenous Base
docs.text: A nitrogen-containing ring compound that projects inward from each sugar toward the helix axis. Bases pair with complementary bases on the opposite strand via hydrogen bonds. Purines (A, G) have two fused rings; pyrimidines (T, C) have one ring. Base stacking between adjacent pairs contributes significantly to helix stability.

docs.title: Adenine (A)
docs.text: A purine base that pairs with Thymine via 2 hydrogen bonds (A=T). Adenine is found in both DNA and RNA (where it pairs with Uracil). It is also the core of ATP and NAD⁺, making it central to energy metabolism.

docs.title: Thymine (T)
docs.text: A pyrimidine base found only in DNA (not RNA). Thymine pairs with Adenine via 2 hydrogen bonds. RNA uses Uracil (U) in place of Thymine. The methyl group on Thymine that distinguishes it from Uracil provides an additional level of DNA stability.

docs.title: Guanine (G)
docs.text: A purine base that pairs with Cytosine via 3 hydrogen bonds (G≡C). The extra hydrogen bond makes G-C-rich DNA regions more resistant to thermal denaturation. Guanine is present in both DNA and RNA.

docs.title: Cytosine (C)
docs.text: A pyrimidine base that pairs with Guanine via 3 hydrogen bonds. Cytosine can be methylated (5-methylcytosine) at CpG dinucleotides — a key epigenetic modification that typically silences gene expression without altering the DNA sequence.

docs.title: Hydrogen Bonds
docs.text: Noncovalent attractions between complementary bases: 2 for A-T pairs, 3 for G-C pairs. Individually weak, but collectively the thousands of hydrogen bonds along a DNA molecule provide stability while still allowing strand separation by helicase during replication and by RNA polymerase during transcription.

docs.title: Major Groove
docs.text: The wider (~22 Å) gap that spirals along the outside of the helix. The major groove exposes the edges of base pairs, enabling transcription factors, repressors, and other regulatory proteins to recognize specific DNA sequences without unwinding the helix — the structural basis of gene regulation.

docs.title: Minor Groove
docs.text: The narrower (~12 Å) gap alternating with the major groove. Less accessible for sequence-specific protein binding, but targeted by certain antibiotics and DNA-staining dyes (e.g., Hoechst 33258). Some structural proteins bind in the minor groove.

docs.title: 3′ End
docs.text: The strand terminus bearing a free 3′ hydroxyl (-OH) group on the deoxyribose. DNA polymerase adds new nucleotides exclusively to the 3′-OH, meaning synthesis always proceeds 5′→3′. The 3′ end is the growing tip of the new strand during replication.

docs.title: 5′ End
docs.text: The strand terminus bearing a free 5′ phosphate group. DNA and RNA sequences are written 5′→3′ by convention. In mRNA, the 5′ end receives the 5′ cap that stabilizes the transcript and facilitates ribosome binding during translation.

docs.title: Endomembrane System — Protein Secretion Pathway
docs.text: View Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text: This interactive diagram traces the journey of a secretory protein through the endomembrane system — from its synthesis on ribosomes at the rough ER, through the Golgi apparatus for processing and sorting, to its release outside the cell via exocytosis. All 13 labeled structures can be explored interactively.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore mode: Hover over any numbered marker or label in the side panel to see a description of that structure, its function in the secretory pathway, and AP exam tips.
  • Quiz mode: Click the Quiz button to test your knowledge. Marker labels are hidden — click the correct marker when prompted to identify each structure.
  • Edit mode: Open main.html?edit=true to calibrate marker positions by dragging them onto the image.

docs.title: Structures in This Diagram
docs.text:
1. Nucleus — Houses DNA; mRNA for secretory proteins is transcribed here
  2. Nuclear pores — Regulate mRNA export and protein import
  3. Rough endoplasmic reticulum — Site of co-translational translocation and initial glycosylation
  4. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum — Lipid synthesis and detoxification (not directly in secretory pathway)
  5. COPII transport vesicle — Carries proteins from ER to cis Golgi
  6. Golgi apparatus (cis face) — Receiving side; quality control
  7. Golgi apparatus (medial cisternae) — Further glycosylation and modification
  8. Golgi apparatus (trans face) — Sorting and packaging into destination-specific vesicles
  9. Secretory vesicle — Carries proteins to the plasma membrane for export
  10. Lysosome — Digestive vesicle receiving enzymes tagged with mannose-6-phosphate
  11. Plasma membrane — Final destination for exocytosis
  12. Exocytosis site — Vesicle fusion releases contents extracellularly
  13. Free ribosomes — Synthesize cytoplasmic proteins (not part of secretory pathway)

docs.title: The Secretory Pathway in Order
docs.text: \[\text{Nucleus} \rightarrow \text{Rough ER} \rightarrow \text{COPII vesicle} \rightarrow \text{cis Golgi} \rightarrow \text{medial Golgi} \rightarrow \text{trans Golgi} \rightarrow \text{Secretory vesicle} \rightarrow \text{Exocytosis}\]

docs.title: Image Prompt: Endomembrane System — Protein Secretion Pathway
Image Prompt: Endomembrane System — Protein Secretion Pathway
Critical Rules
docs.text: No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image.

docs.title: Image Specifications
docs.text:
• Aspect ratio: landscape 4:3
  • Resolution: 1200 × 900 px
  • Style: biological textbook illustration, clean line art with light color fills, white background, AP Biology high school level
  • Background: clean white, no decorative elements

docs.title: Subject
docs.text: A schematic cross-section of a eukaryotic animal cell focused on the endomembrane system and the protein secretion pathway. The diagram should show the spatial relationships between the nucleus, rough ER, smooth ER, Golgi apparatus, transport vesicles, lysosomes, and plasma membrane. Small vesicles should be visible between compartments to suggest the transport pathway, but NO arrows or text.

docs.title: Structure Descriptions and Positions
docs.text:
• Nucleus — Large dark blue oval with visible double-membrane nuclear envelope and nuclear pores; positioned in the upper-left quadrant of the cell; color: #2C3E80. Must have at least 50 px of clear, non-overlapping visual space.

  • Nuclear pores — Small gap-like openings in the nuclear envelope visible at several points around the nucleus; color: #1A5276. At least 3 pores visible as distinct breaks in the double membrane.

  • Rough endoplasmic reticulum — Network of blue-purple folded membrane cisternae studded with small dark dots (ribosomes) on the outer surface; extends from the nuclear envelope toward the center-right of the cell; color: #7E57C2. Must be visibly connected to the nuclear envelope. At least 40 px of clear space for a callout marker.

  • Smooth endoplasmic reticulum — Tubular membrane network continuous with rough ER but WITHOUT ribosome dots; positioned below/right of the rough ER; color: #9B59B6. Visually distinct from rough ER (no dots, more tubular).

  • COPII transport vesicle — Small round vesicle (circle) with a faint textured coat, positioned between the rough ER and the cis face of the Golgi; color: #48C9B0. At least 2 vesicles visible in this region.

  • Golgi apparatus (cis face) — The receiving side of the Golgi stack, facing the ER; left-most cisterna of the Golgi stack; color: #F7DC6F. The cis face should appear slightly convex toward the ER.

  • Golgi apparatus (medial cisternae) — The middle 2-3 cisternae of the Golgi stack; positioned in the center-right of the cell; color: #F5A623. Stacked flattened sacs, slightly curved.

  • Golgi apparatus (trans face) — The shipping side of the Golgi stack, facing the plasma membrane; right-most cisterna; color: #E67E22. Vesicles should appear to bud from this face.

  • Secretory vesicle — Medium-sized round vesicle budding from the trans Golgi and positioned between the Golgi and the plasma membrane; color: #2ECC71. At least 2 vesicles visible moving toward the membrane.

  • Lysosome — Small dark orange-brown sphere with visible granular content inside; positioned near the trans Golgi but separate from the secretory vesicles; color: #D35400. At least 1-2 visible.

  • Plasma membrane — Thin blue phospholipid bilayer forming the outer boundary of the cell along the bottom and right edges; color: #5DADE2. One area should show a vesicle fusing with the membrane (exocytosis), with the membrane slightly bulging outward.

  • Exocytosis site — A region of the plasma membrane where a secretory vesicle is fusing and releasing its contents to the extracellular space; color: #27AE60. The vesicle membrane should be merging with the plasma membrane.

  • Ribosomes (free) — Tiny dark gray dots scattered in the cytoplasm away from the ER; color: #555555. Clearly smaller and separate from the ribosomes on the rough ER.

  • Cytoplasm — Light cream/pale yellow background fill of the entire cell interior; color: #FFF8E7. Provides contrast for all organelles.

docs.title: Spatial Layout Requirements
docs.text:
• The nucleus occupies the upper-left ~25% of the cell area
  • The rough ER extends from the nuclear envelope toward the center
  • The smooth ER is below/right of the rough ER
  • The Golgi apparatus is in the center-right, oriented with cis face toward the ER and trans face toward the plasma membrane
  • Transport vesicles are visible between ER → Golgi and Golgi → plasma membrane
  • The plasma membrane runs along the bottom and right edges
  • Lysosomes are near the trans Golgi but clearly separate
  • The overall flow suggests left-to-right movement: Nucleus → ER → Golgi → Plasma membrane

docs.title: What NOT to Include
docs.text:
• No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image
  • No figure captions, scale bars, or legends
  • No gradient fills that blur structure boundaries
  • No artistic flourishes, bokeh, or photorealistic lighting
  • No mitochondria, cytoskeleton, or other organelles not in the endomembrane system

REPEAT: No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image.

docs.title: Timeline of Evolutionary Thought
docs.text: Run the Timeline of Evolutionary Thought Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text: This interactive timeline traces the development of evolutionary thinking from Carl Linnaeus's classification system in 1735 through the completion of the Human Genome Project in 2003. Events are color-coded by era: Pre-Darwin (gray), Darwin Era (green), Modern Synthesis (blue), and Molecular Era (purple).

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Hover over any event to see a context tooltip with AP Biology connections.
  2. Click an event to expand its full description and AP exam context in the detail panel below the timeline.
  3. Filter by era using the category buttons to focus on a specific period.
  4. Navigate with the pan (arrows) and zoom (+/−) buttons, or drag the timeline to pan.
  5. Fit All resets the view to show all events.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: 9-12 (AP Biology)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Basic understanding of what evolution means in a biological context.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Students explore the full timeline, clicking on each event to read descriptions. Ask: "Which ideas influenced Darwin the most?"
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Use the filter buttons to isolate one era at a time. For each era, discuss how the ideas built on previous work.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Students answer: "Why was Mendel's work important even though Darwin never knew about it?" and "How did the Modern Synthesis resolve the conflict between genetics and natural selection?"

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Students can list 3 pre-Darwin influences on evolutionary thought.
  • Students can explain why deep geological time was necessary for Darwin's theory.
  • Students can describe how Mendelian genetics completed Darwin's theory.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. AP Biology Course and Exam Description — College Board
  2. Evolution — Wikipedia
  3. History of Evolutionary Thought — Wikipedia

docs.title: Glycolysis Pathway Simulator
docs.text: Run the Glycolysis Pathway Simulator MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text: This simulation visualizes the glycolytic pathway as two color-coded halves: the ATP-investment steps (1–5) and the ATP/NADH-producing payoff steps (6–10). Each block lists the substrate, enzyme, and product; badges flag when ATP is consumed or produced and when NADH is generated. Clicking a step reveals the full reaction equation, energetic notes, and cofactors so students can trace how glucose becomes pyruvate and why glycolysis nets only two ATP.

docs.title: Visual Highlights
docs.text:
• Phase backgrounds: Light coral vs. light green regions emphasize energy flow and can be spotlighted with the toggle button.
  • Badges: Red “−ATP,” green “+ATP,” and blue “+NADH” badges signal energy transactions at a glance (×2 in the payoff phase).
  • Cleavage divider: A central column labels the split into two glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate molecules.
  • Net tally cards: Bottom summary cards track cumulative ATP, NADH, and pyruvate yields.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Begin with the Investment phase highlighted (default). Read down steps 1–5 to see where ATP is consumed.
  2. Click any step to open its reaction card. Encourage students to articulate enzyme names aloud.
  3. Press Show Payoff Phase to highlight steps 6–10; discuss why ATP production occurs twice per glucose.
  4. Use the Reset button to clear selections and re-focus the Investment half for review.
  5. Challenge students to explain the net ATP count by referencing the badge placements and the summary panel.

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text:
You can add this MicroSim to any web page by adding this to your HTML:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/biology/sims/glycolysis-simulator/main.html"
        height="1000px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Describe the substrates, enzymes, and products of each glycolytic reaction (Bloom L2).
  • Distinguish between the energy investment and payoff phases by identifying when ATP is used or generated.
  • Explain why glycolysis yields a net of +2 ATP and +2 NADH per glucose.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Show Payoff Phase / Show Investment Phase: Toggles which half of the pathway is emphasized.
  • Reset: Returns to the default emphasis (investment phase) and clears any selected reaction card.
  • Clickable Steps: Selecting a step opens an information card that lists the reaction equation, cofactor needs, and energetic notes.

docs.title: Data and Reactions
docs.text:
Step Enzyme Key Reaction Energy Note 1 Hexokinase Glucose + ATP → Glucose-6-P + ADP −ATP 3 Phosphofructokinase-1 F6P + ATP → F1,6-BP + ADP −ATP 6 G3P dehydrogenase G3P + NAD⁺ + Pi → 1,3-BPG + NADH + H⁺ +2 NADH 7 Phosphoglycerate kinase 1,3-BPG + ADP → 3-PG + ATP +2 ATP 10 Pyruvate kinase PEP + ADP → Pyruvate + ATP +2 ATP

All other steps rearrange carbon skeletons or generate high-energy intermediates that set up these energy transactions. The net outcome shown in the tally cards is +2 ATP, +2 NADH, and 2 Pyruvate per glucose.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: 9–12 (AP/IB Biology) and introductory undergraduate biology

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Students know the purpose of cellular respiration and the role of NADH.
  • Students can define substrate-level phosphorylation.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Engage (4 min): Ask learners to predict why glycolysis costs ATP even though it makes ATP. Display the investment side to confirm.
  2. Explore (7 min): Students click each step, jotting enzyme names and energy changes; toggle to the payoff phase midway.
  3. Explain (4 min): Groups summarize why net ATP is +2 despite two ATP-producing steps happening twice.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Quick exit ticket: “Which steps consume ATP and which produce it?”
  • Oral check: “What reaction generates NADH in glycolysis, and why is it doubled?”
  • Optional screenshot annotation: label the cleavage divider and describe what it represents.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Freeman, S. Biological Science, 7e. Pearson, 2024 — Cellular respiration chapter.
  2. Nelson, D. & Cox, M. Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry, 8e. W.H. Freeman, 2021.
  3. Alberts, B. Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7e. Garland Science, 2022.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text: This MicroSim provides an interactive step-through visualization of the Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle), the central metabolic pathway that oxidizes acetyl-CoA to \(\ce{CO2}\) while generating electron carriers (\(\ce{NADH}\) and \(\ce{FADH2}\)) and a small amount of ATP. The cycle's eight intermediates are arranged in a circular layout with product badges on each reaction arrow.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Step Forward — Click to advance through the cycle one reaction at a time. Each step highlights the active reaction arrow and updates the running tally of products (CO₂, NADH, FADH₂, ATP).
  2. Run Full Cycle — Automatically animates all 8 steps in sequence.
  3. Reset — Returns the cycle to its initial state and clears the tally.
  4. ×2 for glucose — Toggles the tally between "per turn" and "per glucose" (since each glucose produces 2 acetyl-CoA and thus 2 turns of the cycle).
  5. Click any intermediate node — Shows its name, carbon count, and biological role in an info panel.

docs.title: Meiosis Stages Explorer
docs.text: View Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This interactive diagram shows all stages of meiosis in two rows: Meiosis I (top row) and Meiosis II (bottom row). Sixteen callout markers highlight key structures and concepts across all 9 stages, from interphase through the production of four genetically unique haploid cells.

Use Explore mode to hover over any marker or label and read detailed descriptions including AP Exam Tips.

Switch to Quiz mode to test your ability to identify meiotic structures and concepts.

docs.title: Meiosis I (Reductional Division)
docs.text:
Interphase

  1. Unreplicated chromosomes (2n) — Diffuse chromatin; DNA replicates during S phase

Prophase I

  1. Synapsis and tetrad formation — Homologs pair up to form bivalents
  2. Crossing over (chiasmata) — Non-sister chromatids exchange segments

Metaphase I

  1. Bivalents at metaphase plate — Paired homologs align at the cell equator
  2. Independent assortment — Random orientation of each bivalent

Anaphase I

  1. Homolog separation — Homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles
  2. Sister chromatids still joined — Centromeric cohesin protected by shugoshin

Telophase I / Cytokinesis I

  1. Two haploid cells (n) — Each with n chromosomes, still as sister chromatids

docs.title: Meiosis II (Equational Division)
docs.text:
Prophase II

  1. New spindle formation — Spindle assembles in each haploid cell

Metaphase II

  1. Individual chromatid alignment — Chromosomes align at metaphase plate (no bivalents)

Anaphase II

  1. Sister chromatid separation — Centromeric cohesin cleaved; V-shaped chromatids separate

Telophase II / Cytokinesis II

  1. Four unique haploid cells — Genetically distinct due to crossing over and independent assortment
  2. Recombinant chromosomes — Mixed maternal/paternal segments from crossing over

docs.title: Conceptual Markers
docs.text:
1. Reductional division (Meiosis I) — Halves chromosome number (2n → n)
  2. Equational division (Meiosis II) — Separates sister chromatids (n → n)
  3. Nondisjunction risk — Failure of chromosomes to separate causes aneuploidy

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (default): Hover over any numbered marker or label to see a description and AP Exam Tip
  2. Quiz mode: Click the Quiz button — labels are hidden and you must click the correct marker for each prompted structure
  3. Edit mode: Open main.html?edit=true in a browser to drag markers and calibrate positions

docs.text:

  2. Comparison (5 min): Students identify the key differences between anaphase I (homologs separate, X-shaped) and anaphase II (sister chromatids separate, V-shaped)

Meiosis Stages Explorer — Image Generation Prompt

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Create a biological textbook illustration showing all stages of meiosis arranged in two horizontal rows. The top row shows Meiosis I (5 stages) and the bottom row shows Meiosis II (4 stages). A thin horizontal light gray divider line separates the two rows.

docs.title: Technical Specifications
docs.text:
• Aspect ratio: landscape 4:3
  • Resolution: 1200 × 900 px
  • Style: biological textbook illustration, clean line art with light color fills, white background, AP Biology high school level
  • No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
• Top row (~48% of image height): Five cells arranged left to right showing Meiosis I stages: Interphase → Prophase I → Metaphase I → Anaphase I → Telophase I/Cytokinesis I
  • Bottom row (~48% of image height): Four cells arranged left to right showing Meiosis II stages: Prophase II → Metaphase II → Anaphase II → Telophase II/Cytokinesis II
  • Thin vertical light gray divider lines separate each stage within a row
  • Thin horizontal light gray divider line between the two rows
  • Each cell is drawn as a large rounded shape centered in its panel

docs.title: Chromosome Convention
docs.text: Use 2n = 4 (two homologous pairs). Color-code by parental origin: - Maternal chromosomes: Pink/red shades (#D94A4A for one pair, #E57373 for the other) - Paternal chromosomes: Blue shades (#4A90D9 for one pair, #64B5F6 for the other) - After crossing over in Prophase I, recombinant segments show striped pink-blue pattern

docs.title: Panel 1 — Interphase (leftmost ~20%)
docs.text:
• Cell outline: large circle, light gray border, pale cream fill
  • Chromosomes: 4 thin, diffuse chromatin threads (2 pink/red, 2 blue) — NOT condensed, just loose wavy lines spread throughout the nucleus
  • Nuclear envelope: complete dark gray circle
  • Nucleolus: small dark purple circle inside
  • Centrosomes: single orange dot near the nuclear envelope (not yet duplicated visually)

docs.title: Panel 2 — Prophase I (~20%)
docs.text:
• Cell outline: large circle, light gray border, pale cream fill
  • Chromosomes: 4 condensed X-shaped sister chromatids, paired into 2 tetrads (bivalents). Each tetrad shows one pink/red chromosome tightly paired alongside one blue chromosome. At the contact point between homologs, show a small chiasma (X-shaped crossover point) with color mixing
  • Centrosomes: two orange circles migrating to opposite sides
  • Spindle fibers: thin green lines beginning to radiate from centrosomes
  • Nuclear envelope: dark gray dashed circle, beginning to fragment (gaps visible)

docs.title: Panel 3 — Metaphase I (center ~20%)
docs.text:
• Cell outline: large circle, light gray border, pale cream fill
  • Chromosomes: 2 tetrads (bivalents) aligned at the metaphase plate (vertical center line). Each tetrad shows homologous pair side by side — one pink/red, one blue. Chiasmata still visible
  • Spindle fibers: green lines from orange centrosomes at left and right poles, attached to the kinetochores of homologous chromosomes (NOT individual chromatids)
  • Metaphase plate: subtle dashed magenta vertical line at center
  • No nuclear envelope

docs.title: Panel 4 — Anaphase I (~20%)
docs.text:
• Cell outline: slightly elongated oval, light gray border, pale cream fill
  • Chromosomes: Homologous pairs separating — 2 pink/red X-shaped chromosomes moving left, 2 blue X-shaped chromosomes moving right. Sister chromatids are STILL joined (each chromosome is still X-shaped, not V-shaped). Some chromosomes show recombinant segments (mixed pink-blue coloring from crossing over)
  • Spindle fibers: green lines pulling homologs to opposite poles
  • Cell is visibly stretching

docs.title: Panel 5 — Telophase I / Cytokinesis I (rightmost ~20%)
docs.text:
• Two cells pinching apart with a cleavage furrow between them
  • Left cell: contains 2 pink/red X-shaped chromosomes (still as sister chromatids joined at centromere), with some recombinant blue segments
  • Right cell: contains 2 blue X-shaped chromosomes (still as sister chromatids), with some recombinant pink segments
  • Nuclear envelopes: dark gray circles beginning to reform around each chromosome set
  • Cleavage furrow: pink contractile ring pinching at the center

docs.title: Panel 6 — Prophase II (leftmost ~25%)
docs.text:
• Two smaller cells side by side (products of Meiosis I)
  • Left cell: 2 condensed X-shaped chromosomes (pink/red, some with recombinant segments), orange centrosomes at poles, thin green spindle fibers forming, nuclear envelope fragmenting (dashed)
  • Right cell: 2 condensed X-shaped chromosomes (blue, some with recombinant segments), same spindle formation

docs.title: Panel 7 — Metaphase II (~25%)
docs.text:
• Two smaller cells side by side
  • Left cell: 2 X-shaped chromosomes aligned at metaphase plate (vertical center), green spindle fibers from orange centrosomes attached to individual kinetochores of sister chromatids
  • Right cell: same arrangement with blue chromosomes
  • Dashed magenta metaphase plate line visible in each cell

docs.title: Panel 8 — Anaphase II (~25%)
docs.text:
• Two smaller cells side by side, each slightly elongated
  • Left cell: 4 individual V-shaped chromatids (no longer X-shaped) — 2 moving left, 2 moving right. Pink/red with some recombinant blue segments. Green spindle fibers pulling them apart
  • Right cell: same with blue chromatids, some recombinant pink segments

docs.title: Panel 9 — Telophase II / Cytokinesis II (rightmost ~25%)
docs.text:
• Four small haploid cells arranged in a 2×2 cluster
  • Each cell contains 2 single chromatids (not X-shaped anymore — just simple rod shapes) representing n = 2
  • Due to crossing over, each cell has a unique combination of maternal and paternal segments — no two cells are identical in their color patterns
  • Nuclear envelopes: complete dark gray circles in each cell
  • Cleavage furrows: pink pinch marks between dividing cells

docs.title: Color Key (hex values)
docs.text: Structure Color Hex Maternal chromosomes — pair 1 Red #D94A4A Maternal chromosomes — pair 2 Light red #E57373 Paternal chromosomes — pair 1 Blue #4A90D9 Paternal chromosomes — pair 2 Light blue #64B5F6 Recombinant segments Striped pink-blue mixed Spindle fibers / microtubules Green #4CAF50 Nuclear envelope Dark gray #555555 Centrosomes Orange #FF9800 Metaphase plate line Magenta dashed #E91E9F Contractile ring / cleavage furrow Pink #F48FB1 Nucleolus Dark purple #6A1B9A Cell outline Light gray #BDBDBD Cell fill Pale cream #FFF8E1

docs.title: Critical Reminders
docs.text:
• Each structure must have at least 30–40 px of clear landing zone for a callout marker
  • Chromosomes in Anaphase I are STILL X-shaped (sister chromatids joined) — only in Anaphase II do they separate into V-shaped individual chromatids
  • The four final cells must each be visually UNIQUE in chromosome coloring to show genetic diversity from crossing over and independent assortment
  • Keep structures well-separated within each panel
  • Bottom row cells should be noticeably smaller than top row cells

No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image.
