docs.title: Mitochondria & Electron Transport Chain
docs.text:
View Fullscreen

This interactive diagram covers 15 structures of the mitochondrion and the electron transport chain (AP Biology Unit 3). The upper section shows the overall mitochondrial architecture; the lower zoom reveals the five protein complexes of the inner membrane in order of electron flow: Complex I → CoQ → Complex III → Cytochrome c → Complex IV → ATP synthase, with Complex II shown as the alternate FADH₂ entry point.

docs.title: Outer Membrane
docs.text: A smooth, continuous bilayer enclosing the entire mitochondrion. Porins (VDACs) make it freely permeable to molecules up to ~5 kDa. Larger proteins cross via the TOM (Translocase of the Outer Membrane) complex.

docs.title: Inner Membrane
docs.text: A highly impermeable bilayer containing no porins — sealed to all ions including H⁺. Houses all five ETC complexes and ATP synthase. Contains the unique phospholipid cardiolipin and has an unusually high protein-to-lipid ratio (~80% protein). The site of oxidative phosphorylation.

docs.title: Cristae
docs.text: Extensive infoldings of the inner membrane that increase its surface area several-fold, concentrating the ETC complexes. Cristae shape is maintained by MICOS complexes and OPA1; their density correlates with a cell's energy demand.

docs.title: Matrix
docs.text: The aqueous interior enclosed by the inner membrane. Houses the citric acid cycle enzymes, pyruvate dehydrogenase, fatty acid oxidation enzymes, mitochondrial DNA (circular, ~16,569 bp), and mitochondrial ribosomes. NADH and FADH₂ are produced here and feed electrons into the ETC.

docs.title: Intermembrane Space
docs.text: The compartment between the outer and inner membranes. Small solutes (including H⁺) equilibrate with the cytoplasm via outer membrane porins, but the ETC pumps additional H⁺ into the IMS from the matrix, establishing the proton-motive force. The IMS is also the compartment from which cytochrome c is released during apoptosis.

docs.title: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase)
docs.text: The largest ETC complex (~45 subunits). Oxidizes NADH → NAD⁺ in the matrix and reduces CoQ to CoQH₂. Pumps 4 H⁺ into the IMS per 2 electrons. Inhibited by rotenone. The entry point for electrons from NADH produced in the matrix by the citric acid cycle and pyruvate oxidation.

docs.title: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase)
docs.text: The only ETC complex that is also a citric acid cycle enzyme: it oxidizes succinate → fumarate, producing enzyme-bound FADH₂. Electrons pass through FAD and iron-sulfur clusters to CoQ. Does NOT pump H⁺ into the IMS — the reason FADH₂ yields fewer ATP (~1.5) than NADH (~2.5).

docs.title: Coenzyme Q / Ubiquinone (CoQ)
docs.text: A small, hydrophobic mobile carrier that diffuses laterally within the inner membrane lipid bilayer. Collects electrons from both Complex I and Complex II (as CoQH₂) and delivers them to Complex III. The convergence point of NADH and FADH₂ electron inputs. Analogous to plastoquinone (PQ) in chloroplasts.

docs.title: Complex III (cytochrome bc1)
docs.text: Oxidizes CoQH₂ and reduces cytochrome c via the Q-cycle, pumping 4 H⁺ into the IMS per 2 electrons transferred. Contains cytochrome b, cytochrome c1, and the Rieske iron-sulfur protein. Inhibited by antimycin A. Analogous to the cytochrome b6f complex of the chloroplast thylakoid membrane.

docs.title: Cytochrome c
docs.text: A small, soluble heme protein (12 kDa) loosely bound to the outer face of the inner membrane. Shuttles one electron at a time from Complex III to Complex IV within the IMS. When released into the cytoplasm during apoptosis, it binds Apaf-1 to activate caspase-9. Analogous to plastocyanin in chloroplasts.

docs.title: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase)
docs.text: The terminal complex of the ETC. Accepts 4 electrons from 4 cytochrome c molecules and reduces \(\ce{O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O}\) in the matrix. Pumps 4 H⁺ into the IMS per O₂ reduced. Contains copper (CuA, CuB) and heme (cyt a, cyt a3) centers. Inhibited by cyanide, carbon monoxide, and azide.

docs.title: ATP Synthase (Complex V)
docs.text: Uses the proton-motive force — H⁺ flowing from IMS → matrix through the F₀ transmembrane channel — to synthesize ATP via the F₁ catalytic head in the matrix. The F₀ c-ring rotates as H⁺ passes through, driving conformational changes in F₁ β-subunits (binding change mechanism; ~2.7 H⁺ per ATP). Inhibited by oligomycin. Compare with CF₁ in chloroplasts: identical mechanism, opposite H⁺ flow direction (lumen → stroma vs. IMS → matrix).

docs.title: NADH / FADH₂ Inputs
docs.text: The electron-carrying products of glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, and the citric acid cycle that feed the ETC. NADH delivers electrons to Complex I; FADH₂ delivers to Complex II. Per glucose: 10 NADH and 2 FADH₂ are produced across all stages. NADH yields ~2.5 ATP; FADH₂ yields ~1.5 ATP via oxidative phosphorylation.

docs.title: H⁺ Proton Gradient
docs.text: The proton-motive force (PMF) across the inner membrane has two components: a chemical gradient (ΔpH ≈ 1 unit) and an electrical potential (ΔΨ ≈ −180 mV, matrix negative). Complexes I, III, and IV each pump 4 H⁺ into the IMS per O₂ reduced (12 H⁺ total). H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase to drive ATP synthesis (chemiosmosis, Mitchell hypothesis).

docs.title: O₂ → H₂O (Final Electron Acceptor)
docs.text: Molecular oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor at Complex IV. \(\ce{O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O}\) — the very negative reduction potential of this reaction (\(E°' = +0.82\text{ V}\)) pulls electrons through the entire ETC. Without O₂, the chain backs up, NAD⁺ and FAD are depleted, and aerobic metabolism halts.

docs.title: Mitosis Stage Explorer
docs.text: View Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This interactive diagram shows the five stages of mitosis — Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase, and Cytokinesis — in a single panoramic view. Each stage is shown as a separate cell with key structures labeled by numbered callout markers.

Use Explore mode to hover over any marker or label and read detailed descriptions of each structure, including AP Exam Tips for testable concepts.

Switch to Quiz mode to test your ability to identify mitotic structures by clicking the correct marker when prompted.

docs.title: Prophase
docs.text:
1. Condensing chromosomes — Chromatin coils into visible X-shaped sister chromatids
  2. Centrosomes with asters — Microtubule-organizing centers migrate to opposite poles
  3. Nuclear envelope breakdown — Lamina disassembles as CDKs phosphorylate lamins
  4. Disappearing nucleolus — rRNA transcription ceases and the nucleolus disperses

docs.title: Metaphase
docs.text:
1. Metaphase plate alignment — All chromosomes bi-orient at the cell equator
  2. Kinetochore microtubules — Spindle fibers attach to chromosome kinetochores from both poles
  3. Spindle assembly checkpoint — SAC ensures all kinetochores are properly attached before anaphase

docs.title: Anaphase
docs.text:
1. Sister chromatid separation — Separase cleaves cohesin; V-shaped chromatids move to poles
  2. Cell elongation — Polar microtubules slide apart, pushing the cell poles further away

docs.title: Telophase
docs.text:
1. Reforming nuclear envelopes — Membrane vesicles fuse around each chromosome set
  2. Chromosome decondensation — Condensed chromosomes relax back into diffuse chromatin
  3. Cleavage furrow — Cell surface indents at the former metaphase plate position
  4. Contractile ring — Actin-myosin belt constricts to pinch the cell in two

docs.title: Cytokinesis
docs.text:
1. Daughter cells — Two genetically identical diploid cells, each half the parent's size
  2. Restored interphase nuclei — Complete nuclei with decondensed chromatin; cells enter G1

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (default): Hover over any numbered marker or label to see a description and AP Exam Tip
  2. Quiz mode: Click the Quiz button — labels are hidden and you must click the correct marker for each prompted structure
  3. Edit mode: Open main.html?edit=true in a browser to drag markers and calibrate positions

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: 9-12 (AP Biology)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Basic understanding of the cell cycle (G1, S, G2, M phases)
  • Knowledge of chromosome structure (chromatids, centromeres)
  • Familiarity with the cytoskeleton (microtubules, microfilaments)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Students hover over all 15 structures in Explore mode, reading descriptions and AP tips for each stage
  2. Stage Comparison (5 min): Students identify which structures appear, disappear, or change between stages
  3. Quiz Assessment (5 min): Students complete the Quiz mode, identifying all 15 structures by clicking the correct marker

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Students should be able to name the 5 stages of mitosis in order
  • Students should identify at least 3 key events per stage
  • Students should explain the role of the spindle assembly checkpoint
  • Students should compare animal cell cytokinesis (cleavage furrow) with plant cell cytokinesis (cell plate)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Mitosis - Wikipedia
  2. Cell Division - Khan Academy
  3. Campbell Biology, 12th Edition — Chapter 12: The Cell Cycle

Mitosis Stage Explorer — Image Generation Prompt

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Create a biological textbook illustration showing the five stages of mitosis in a single horizontal sequence from left to right: Prophase → Metaphase → Anaphase → Telophase → Cytokinesis. Each stage occupies approximately one-fifth of the image width, separated by thin vertical light gray divider lines.

docs.title: Technical Specifications
docs.text:
• Aspect ratio: landscape 4:3
  • Resolution: 1200 × 900 px
  • Style: biological textbook illustration, clean line art with light color fills, white background, AP Biology high school level
  • No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: Five panels arranged left to right, each showing one cell in the appropriate mitotic stage. Each cell is drawn as a large rounded shape (~180 px wide) centered in its panel with adequate margin above and below for marker placement.

docs.title: Panel 1 — Prophase (leftmost ~20%)
docs.text:
• Cell outline: large oval, light gray border, pale cream fill
  • Chromosomes: 4 condensing X-shaped sister chromatids visible inside the cell; drawn as thick rods in two colors — 2 blue chromosomes and 2 red chromosomes (representing two homologous pairs). Chromosomes are randomly distributed within the cell.
  • Centrosomes: two small orange circles at opposite sides of the cell, with thin green lines (spindle fibers) beginning to radiate outward from each
  • Nuclear envelope: dark gray dashed circle around the chromosomes, partially fragmented (gaps visible on left and right sides) to show it is breaking down
  • Nucleolus: small dark purple circle inside the nuclear envelope area, fading/partially transparent to show it is disappearing

docs.title: Panel 2 — Metaphase (left-center ~20%)
docs.text:
• Cell outline: large oval, light gray border, pale cream fill
  • Chromosomes: 4 fully condensed X-shaped sister chromatids perfectly aligned in a single vertical line at the center of the cell (the metaphase plate). Same blue/red color coding as Prophase.
  • Metaphase plate: shown as the vertical alignment zone — a subtle dashed magenta vertical line at center
  • Spindle apparatus: thin green lines (kinetochore microtubules) extending from two orange centrosomes at left and right poles to the kinetochore (center) of each chromosome
  • No nuclear envelope — completely gone

docs.title: Panel 3 — Anaphase (center ~20%)
docs.text:
• Cell outline: elongated oval (wider than other panels), light gray border, pale cream fill — the cell is visibly stretching horizontally
  • Chromosomes: 8 individual chromatids (4 moving left, 4 moving right) pulled toward opposite poles. Each chromatid is V-shaped with the centromere leading. Left set: 2 blue + 2 red. Right set: 2 blue + 2 red.
  • Spindle fibers: green lines from each centrosome (orange circles at poles) attached to the V-point of each chromatid, visibly shortened compared to metaphase
  • Polar microtubules: additional green lines overlapping at the cell center, pushing the poles apart

docs.title: Panel 4 — Telophase (right-center ~20%)
docs.text:
• Cell outline: elongated pinched shape — a cleavage furrow is forming at the center (waist narrowing)
  • Chromosomes: at each pole, chromosomes are decondensing — drawn as looser, more diffuse blobs rather than distinct X or V shapes. Still blue/red colored but less defined.
  • Nuclear envelopes: two new dark gray dashed circles reforming around each cluster of chromosomes at the two poles
  • Cleavage furrow: visible indentation at the center of the cell, with a ring of small pink dots representing the actin-myosin contractile ring
  • Spindle remnants: faint green lines, mostly disappeared

docs.title: Panel 5 — Cytokinesis (rightmost ~20%)
docs.text:

docs.title: Neuron Structure
docs.text:
View Fullscreen

This interactive diagram covers the 13 key structures of a multipolar motor neuron (AP Biology Unit 5 — Nervous System). The main view shows the full neuron from dendrites through the myelinated axon to the axon terminals, with a synaptic inset revealing the ultrastructure of the chemical synapse.

docs.title: Cell body (soma)
docs.text: The metabolic center of the neuron, containing the nucleus and all organelles (rough ER / Nissl bodies, Golgi, mitochondria) that sustain the cell's enormous protein synthesis demand. All proteins used in axons and dendrites are made here.

docs.title: Nucleus
docs.text: Houses the neuronal genome and directs transcription of genes for ion channels, receptors, and neurotransmitter-synthesizing enzymes. The prominent nucleolus reflects the high ribosome demand needed to maintain a cell that may extend over 1 meter.

docs.title: Dendrites
docs.text: The primary input zone. Branching processes covered in dendritic spines receive neurotransmitter signals from thousands of presynaptic neurons, generating local graded potentials (EPSPs and IPSPs) that travel toward the soma. More branching = greater computational capacity.

docs.title: Axon hillock
docs.text: The spike initiation zone — a cone-shaped region at the soma-axon junction with the highest density of voltage-gated \(\ce{Na+}\) channels. All graded potentials from dendrites are summed here; if the net depolarization reaches threshold (~−55 mV), an action potential fires (all-or-nothing law).

docs.title: Axon
docs.text: The output cable of the neuron. Conducts action potentials from the axon hillock to the terminals without decrement (signal strength does not weaken with distance). Microtubule tracks inside the axoplasm serve as rails for bidirectional axonal transport of vesicles and organelles (kinesin for anterograde, dynein for retrograde).

docs.title: Myelin sheath
docs.text: A multilayered spiral wrap of Schwann cell (PNS) or oligodendrocyte (CNS) plasma membrane around the axon. The high-lipid composition (~70–80% lipid) creates excellent electrical insulation, enabling saltatory conduction — action potentials jump node to node, increasing speed up to 100× and reducing \(\ce{Na+}\) entry (and therefore ATP needed for the \(\ce{Na+}\)/\(\ce{K+}\)-ATPase).

docs.title: Schwann cell
docs.text: The myelinating glial cell of the peripheral nervous system. Each Schwann cell forms one internodal myelin segment by spiraling its plasma membrane around the axon. Schwann cells also support PNS nerve regeneration after injury — unlike oligodendrocytes in the CNS.

docs.title: Node of Ranvier
docs.text: A 1–2 µm gap between adjacent myelin segments where the axon is exposed and densely packed with voltage-gated \(\ce{Na+}\) and \(\ce{K+}\) channels. Saltatory conduction regenerates the action potential only at nodes, skipping the insulated internodal regions and greatly reducing ion flux per action potential.

docs.title: Axon terminals (boutons)
docs.text: Swollen presynaptic knobs at the ends of axon branches. Each bouton contains synaptic vesicles, abundant mitochondria (to power vesicle cycling), and voltage-gated \(\ce{Ca^2+}\) channels. When an action potential arrives, \(\ce{Ca^2+}\) influx triggers neurotransmitter exocytosis.

docs.title: Synaptic vesicles
docs.text: Small (~40–50 nm) membrane-bound organelles packed with neurotransmitter (e.g., acetylcholine, glutamate, GABA, dopamine). When \(\ce{Ca^2+}\) enters the terminal, SNARE proteins (synaptobrevin + syntaxin + SNAP-25) mediate vesicle fusion with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter into the cleft by exocytosis.

docs.title: Synaptic cleft
docs.text: The ~20–40 nm extracellular gap between the presynaptic terminal and the postsynaptic membrane. Neurotransmitter diffuses across this gap. The cleft contains degrading enzymes (e.g., acetylcholinesterase) and adhesion proteins (neuroligins, neurexins) that hold the synapse together. Many drugs act here — SSRIs block serotonin reuptake; organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase.

docs.title: Postsynaptic membrane
docs.text: The region of the target cell membrane (dendrite, soma, or muscle) facing the cleft. Thickened by the postsynaptic density (PSD), a protein scaffold that anchors receptors. Neurotransmitter binding here either opens ion channels directly (ionotropic receptors) or activates G-protein cascades (metabotropic receptors).

docs.title: Receptor proteins
docs.text: Integral membrane proteins in the postsynaptic membrane that bind specific neurotransmitters with high affinity. Ionotropic receptors (AMPA, NMDA, nicotinic ACh) are ligand-gated ion channels — fast, direct response. Metabotropic receptors (GABA-B, muscarinic ACh, all GPCRs) produce slower but more diverse and amplified intracellular responses via second-messenger cascades.

docs.title: Interactive pH scale explorer
docs.text: Run the pH Explorer MicroSim fullscreen Edit the pH Explorer MicroSim using the p5.js editor

docs.title: About this MicroSim
docs.text: Move a vertical cursor across a 0–14 pH scale to see color-coded pins for real substances (gastric acid, lemon juice, blood, seawater, bleach, etc.). As you slide, a live panel displays pH, pOH, \([\ce{H^+}]\), \([\ce{OH^-}]\), and an acidity/basicity description, reinforcing how logarithmic concentration changes map onto everyday chemicals.

docs.title: How to use
docs.text:
1. Drag the pH slider (0–14, step 0.1) or click the scale to move the cursor.
  2. Watch the [H⁺], [OH⁻], and pOH readings update automatically (\([\ce{H^+}] = 10^{-\text{pH}}\)).
  3. Compare the cursor color and text classification (strongly acidic, neutral, strongly basic).
  4. Hover over or simply read the pinned labels to contextualize where common substances fall.

docs.title: Classroom ideas
docs.text:
• Give students a list of pH values and have them match each to a real substance on the scale.
  • Ask learners to predict [H⁺] for a given pH, then verify it in the panel and note how doubling the pH reduces [H⁺] by 100×.
  • Use the classification text to spark discussion about the differences between weakly and strongly acidic/basic solutions.
  • Build lab prework: students locate buffer pH targets and explain why the color region matters.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text: Item Details Subject area Chemistry — acid-base theory Grade band Grades 10–12 and introductory college Learning objective Students will interpret the pH scale to identify relative acidity/basicity and convert between pH, pOH, \([\ce{H^+}]\), and \([\ce{OH^-}]\). Bloom's level Apply Duration 8–10 minutes Prerequisites Logarithmic pH definition, conjugate acid/base knowledge Assessment ideas Quick journal entry: “At pH 5, what are [H⁺], [OH⁻], pOH, and a real-world example?”

docs.title: Instructional design review
docs.text:
• Single objective: “Students use the pH scale to relate colors, examples, and quantitative conversions.” ✔️
  • Control inventory: one slider plus the responsive info panel (no extra buttons).
  • Progressive disclosure: only the selected cursor data updates; pins remain as context.
  • Accessibility: large fonts, color + labels, slider accessible via keyboard.

docs.title: Grade level
docs.text: High school chemistry (Unit on acids/bases) or introductory college

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-minute exploration or bell-ringer

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Definition of pH/pOH
  • Relationship between [H⁺], [OH⁻], Kw

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm-up (3 min): Instructor demonstrates the gradient and pins.
  2. Student exploration (5 min): Learners slide to three specific pH values and record all computed quantities.
  3. Wrap-up (2 min): Share how a unit change on the pH scale affects concentration (×10).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Exit ticket: “If blood is pH 7.4, what is [H⁺]? Where does household ammonia fall relative to blood?”
  • Extension: Students screenshot a region (e.g., weakly basic) and annotate it with two examples.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Tro, N. J. Chemistry: A Molecular Approach, 5th ed., Pearson, 2020 — pH scale fundamentals.
  2. Zumdahl & Zumdahl. Chemistry, 11th ed., Cengage, 2020 — pH/pOH conversions and typical household examples.

docs.title: Plant Cell Drawing
docs.text:
View the Animal Cell MicroSim Fullscreen

The six major plant cell components shown in the generated illustration are:

docs.title: Cell Wall
docs.text: The thick outermost green boundary that gives the plant cell its rigid shape and structural support.

docs.title: Cell Membrane
docs.text: The thin inner boundary just inside the cell wall that regulates what enters and leaves the cell.

docs.title: Nucleus
docs.text: The large purple spherical organelle containing the genetic material (DNA), with a darker nucleolus inside.

docs.title: Central Vacuole
docs.text: The large light-blue sac occupying much of the cell’s interior, responsible for water storage, turgor pressure, and storage of dissolved substances.

docs.title: Chloroplast
docs.text: The green oval organelle with internal stacked membrane structures (thylakoids), responsible for photosynthesis.

docs.title: Mitochondrion
docs.text: The smaller teal bean-shaped organelle with folded inner membranes (cristae), responsible for cellular respiration and ATP production.

docs.title: Prokaryote vs. Eukaryote Cell Comparison
docs.text: Run the Prokaryote vs. Eukaryote Comparison Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text: This interactive diagram displays a prokaryotic bacterial cell and a eukaryotic animal cell side by side, with 15 labeled structures. Students can explore each structure by hovering over numbered markers or labels to read descriptions and AP Biology exam tips. Quiz mode tests structure identification with immediate feedback and a celebration animation on completion.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode: Hover over any numbered marker on the diagram or click a label in the side panel to read about that structure.
  2. Quiz mode: Click the Quiz button. The infobox will prompt you to click on a named structure. Correct answers reveal the label; incorrect clicks give feedback.
  3. Edit mode: Append ?edit=true to the URL to drag markers and calibrate their positions.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: 9-12 (AP Biology)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15-20 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Basic understanding of cell theory and the difference between living and non-living things.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (7 min): Students hover over each structure on both cells, recording which structures are unique to prokaryotes, unique to eukaryotes, and shared by both.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Ask: "What is the single most important structural difference between prokaryotes and eukaryotes? Why does compartmentalization matter for eukaryotic cell function?"
  3. Assessment (5 min): Students complete Quiz mode, identifying all 15 structures. Discuss: "How does endosymbiotic theory explain the presence of 70S ribosomes in mitochondria?"

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Students can name and locate structures unique to prokaryotes (cell wall, nucleoid, plasmid, flagellum, pili).
  • Students can name and locate structures unique to eukaryotes (nucleus, nucleolus, rough ER, Golgi, mitochondria, lysosomes).
  • Students can identify shared structures (plasma membrane, ribosomes, cytoplasm, DNA) and explain key differences (70S vs. 80S ribosomes, circular vs. linear DNA).
  • Students can explain endosymbiotic theory using evidence from mitochondrial structure.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Prokaryote — Wikipedia
  2. Eukaryote — Wikipedia
  3. Endosymbiotic theory — Wikipedia
  4. AP Biology Course and Exam Description — College Board

docs.title: Prokaryote vs. Eukaryote Cell Comparison — Image Prompt
Prokaryote vs. Eukaryote Cell Comparison — Image Prompt
Purpose
docs.text: Generate a single wide illustration showing a prokaryotic bacterial cell on the left and a eukaryotic animal cell on the right, side by side in a single frame. The image will be used as a background for an interactive MicroSim where students hover over numbered callout markers to learn about each structure. No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image.

docs.title: Global Specifications
docs.text:
• Aspect ratio: 4:3 landscape (1200 × 900 px)
  • Style: Clean biological textbook illustration, precise molecular-level artwork with flat color fills, white background, AP Biology high school level
  • Layout: A single continuous scene with two cells. The prokaryotic cell occupies the left ~40% of the image. The eukaryotic cell occupies the right ~55%. A narrow gap of white space (~5%) separates them.
  • Background: Pure white
  • No text of any kind in the image. No labels, no cell type names, no chemical formulas, no numbers, no arrows, no annotation marks. Repeat: absolutely no text.

docs.title: Color Palette
docs.text: Element Color Hex Cell wall (prokaryote) Tan/sandy brown #D4A574 Plasma membrane (both cells) Medium blue #5DADE2 Cytoplasm (prokaryote) Light yellow-green #F9F3D0 Cytoplasm (eukaryote) Pale peach/cream #FDEBD0 Nucleoid region / circular DNA Teal blue #1ABC9C Nucleus (eukaryote) Dark blue / navy #2C3E80 Nuclear envelope Dark blue outline #1A237E Nucleolus Deep purple #6C3483 Ribosomes (prokaryote, 70S) Dark gray, small dots #555555 Ribosomes (eukaryote, 80S) Dark gray, slightly larger dots #444444 Rough ER Blue-purple with ribosome dots #7E57C2 Smooth ER Light purple #B39DDB Golgi apparatus Gold/amber stacked cisternae #F5A623 Mitochondria Red-orange with cristae #E74C3C Flagellum Dark green #27AE60 Pili Olive green, short stubs #7D8B3E Lysosomes Brown-orange spheres #D35400 Plasmid Small teal ring #16A085

docs.title: Prokaryotic Cell (left side)
docs.text:
Draw a large oval bacterial cell filling the left portion of the image, oriented slightly diagonally (tilted ~15 degrees from horizontal).

  • Cell wall: Thick outer boundary (8-10 px) in tan/sandy brown (#D4A574). Clearly distinguishable from the plasma membrane inside it.
  • Plasma membrane: Thinner inner boundary (4-5 px) in medium blue (#5DADE2), just inside the cell wall with a narrow gap of white between them.
  • Cytoplasm: Light yellow-green (#F9F3D0) fill inside the plasma membrane.
  • Nucleoid region: An irregular, cloud-like zone of teal blue (#1ABC9C) in the center of the cell, NOT enclosed by any membrane. Should look like tangled DNA strands/fibers spreading through the central area, occupying ~25% of the cell interior. The boundary should be diffuse/fuzzy, not sharp — emphasizing that there is NO membrane around it.
  • Circular DNA (chromosome): Within the nucleoid, show one large tangled circular loop of teal DNA.
  • Plasmid: One small separate teal ring (#16A085) near the edge of the nucleoid, clearly a separate small circle of DNA distinct from the main chromosome.
  • Ribosomes (70S): Many tiny dark gray dots (#555555) scattered throughout the cytoplasm, ~40-50 dots visible. They should be SMALL (3-4 px each) to contrast with the larger eukaryotic ribosomes.
  • Flagellum: A single wavy/sinusoidal dark green (#27AE60) line extending from the right end of the cell, about 40% of the cell's length. It should look whip-like and flexible.
  • Pili: 6-8 short olive green (#7D8B3E) stubby projections distributed around the outer surface of the cell wall, much shorter than the flagellum (~10-15% of cell width).
  • No membrane-bound organelles. The interior should be clearly simpler than the eukaryotic cell — just ribosomes, nucleoid DNA, and cytoplasm.

docs.title: Eukaryotic Animal Cell (right side)
docs.text:
Draw a large irregular rounded cell filling the right portion of the image. The shape should be slightly amoeboid — not a perfect circle, with some gentle bumps and indentations.

  • Plasma membrane: Thin boundary (4-5 px) in medium blue (#5DADE2). No cell wall.
  • Cytoplasm: Pale peach/cream (#FDEBD0) fill.
  • Nucleus: A large oval structure (~20% of cell diameter) positioned slightly off-center (upper left quadrant of the cell). Dark blue (#2C3E80) fill with a clearly visible double-membrane nuclear envelope (#1A237E, two parallel lines with nuclear pores shown as small gaps).
  • Nucleolus: A small dense deep purple (#6C3483) circle inside the nucleus, ~25% the diameter of the nucleus.
  • Rough ER: A network of blue-purple (#7E57C2) folded membranes extending from the nuclear envelope toward the cell interior. Show 4-5 parallel wavy membrane sheets with dark gray dots (ribosomes) studding the outer surface. Should visually connect to the nuclear envelope.
  • Smooth ER: A smaller network of light purple (#B39DDB) tubular membranes near the rough ER but WITHOUT ribosome dots. Should look smoother and more tubular.
  • Golgi apparatus: 4-5 stacked gold/amber (#F5A623) curved cisternae (like a stack of pita bread) with small vesicles budding from the ends. Position in the lower-center area of the cell.
  • Mitochondria: 2-3 red-orange (#E74C3C) oval organelles with visible internal cristae (folded inner membrane). Each ~8% of cell diameter. Distribute in different areas of the cytoplasm.
  • Ribosomes (80S): Dark gray dots (#444444) scattered in the cytoplasm, slightly LARGER than the prokaryotic ribosomes (4-5 px each). Also visible on the rough ER surface.
  • Lysosomes: 2-3 small brown-orange (#D35400) spheres scattered in the cytoplasm, each ~4% of cell diameter.

docs.title: Composition Notes
docs.text:
• Both cells should be drawn at approximately the same visual prominence — the prokaryote should not look tiny next to the eukaryote
  • The eukaryotic cell should be ~30% larger than the prokaryotic cell to suggest the actual size difference, but both should fill their respective halves
  • The complexity difference should be visually obvious: the prokaryote has a simple interior (DNA + ribosomes), while the eukaryote has many distinct compartmentalized organelles
  • Each structure must occupy enough image area that a 24 px circular marker dot can be placed on it without touching neighboring structures
  • Use flat color fills with very subtle shading — no heavy gradients, no photorealistic rendering
  • The style should be consistent between both cells — same line weights, same artistic approach

No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image. This is critical — the interactive overlay adds all labels programmatically.

docs.title: Protein Structure Levels Explorer
docs.text: Run the Protein Structure Levels Explorer Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text: This interactive explorer displays the four levels of protein structure side by side: primary (amino acid sequence), secondary (alpha helices and beta sheets), tertiary (3D folding), and quaternary (multi-subunit assembly). Each panel shows a detailed biological illustration with hover-activated descriptions explaining the structures, stabilizing forces, and AP Biology exam relevance.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Hover over any of the four panels to highlight that level and read its description in the infobox below.
  2. Each panel shows the stabilizing forces (peptide bonds, hydrogen bonds, R-group interactions, etc.) that maintain that level of structure.
  3. AP Tips at the bottom of each description highlight common exam questions and misconceptions.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: 9-12 (AP Biology)

docs.title: Duration

docs.title: Prerequisites

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Students hover over each panel from left to right, reading the progression from simple linear chain to complex multi-subunit assembly.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Ask students: "What type of bond stabilizes each level? Why does changing one amino acid in the primary structure affect all higher levels?"
  3. Assessment (5 min): Students answer: "A mutation changes a polar amino acid to a nonpolar one on the protein surface. Which level(s) of structure are affected and why?"

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Students can name and describe all four levels of protein structure.
  • Students can identify which bonds/interactions stabilize each level.
  • Students can explain how denaturation affects tertiary but not primary structure.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Generate a single wide illustration showing the four levels of protein structure side by side in four equal panels. The image will be used as a background for an interactive MicroSim where students hover over each panel to learn about that structural level. No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image.

docs.title: Global Specifications
docs.text:
• Aspect ratio: 4:3 landscape (1600 × 1200 px)
  • Style: Clean biological textbook illustration, precise molecular-level artwork with flat color fills, white background, AP Biology high school level
  • Layout: Four equal-width vertical panels arranged horizontally, separated by thin light-gray divider lines. Each panel contains one level of protein structure.
  • Background: Pure white within each panel
  • No text of any kind in the image. No labels, no level names, no chemical formulas, no numbers, no arrows, no annotation marks. Repeat: absolutely no text.

docs.title: Color Palette (consistent across all panels)
docs.text: Element Color Hex Nonpolar amino acids Warm gray #95A5A6 Polar amino acids Sky blue #5DADE2 Positively charged amino acids Coral red #E74C3C Negatively charged amino acids Orange #E67E22 Peptide bond backbone Dark gray #2C3E50 Hydrogen bonds (dashed) Green #27AE60 Disulfide bridges Gold/yellow #F1C40F Alpha helices Orange-red #E67E22 Beta sheets Blue #3498DB Loops/coils Light gray #BDC3C7 Heme groups Dark red/maroon #922B21 Alpha subunits (quaternary) Light blue #AED6F1 Beta subunits (quaternary) Light pink/salmon #F5B7B1 Oxygen molecules Bright red #E74C3C

docs.title: Panel 1 — Primary Structure (leftmost)
docs.text:
Draw a linear chain of amino acids running horizontally across the panel, slightly curved in a gentle S-shape to fill the vertical space.

  • Chain: 10-12 amino acid residues shown as large, distinct colored circles (diameter ~60-70px) connected by thick dark gray lines representing peptide bonds
  • Amino acid colors: Alternate between nonpolar (warm gray), polar (sky blue), positively charged (coral red), and negatively charged (orange) — use a mix showing that the sequence contains different types
  • Circle appearance: Each amino acid is a solid filled circle with a slightly darker outline of the same hue. No letters or abbreviations inside the circles.
  • Peptide bond connections: Thick dark gray lines (~4px) connecting each circle to the next in sequence. The bonds should be clearly visible between the circles.
  • Chain path: The chain should flow from upper-left to lower-right in a gentle, readable curve — NOT perfectly straight, but with a natural slight wave. This shows it is a linear sequence.
  • N-terminus: The leftmost/top circle should have a small triangular arrow pointing inward (indicating the start of the chain) — just a shape, no text
  • C-terminus: The rightmost/bottom circle should have a small square cap (indicating the end) — just a shape, no text
  • Side chains: Small stubs or bumps projecting outward from each circle in different directions, colored to match their parent amino acid. These represent R-groups but should be simple protrusions, not detailed chemical structures.
  • Visual feel: Clean, colorful beads on a string. The emphasis is on LINEAR SEQUENCE — one amino acid after another.

docs.title: Panel 2 — Secondary Structure
docs.text: Draw two secondary structures side by side within the panel: an alpha helix on the left half and a beta pleated sheet on the right half.

docs.title: Alpha Helix (left half of panel):
docs.text:
• Shape: A right-handed coiled ribbon/helix running vertically, about 5-6 turns visible
  • Ribbon color: Orange-red (#E67E22), with subtle shading to show the 3D coil — the front of the ribbon is brighter, the back is slightly darker
  • Ribbon width: Thick enough to clearly see the helical coil pattern (~30px wide ribbon)
  • Hydrogen bonds: Green dashed lines running vertically along the interior of the helix, connecting one turn to another (every 3.6 residues). Show 4-5 green dashed lines visible between coil turns. These should be clearly visible as dashed green lines, not solid.
  • R-group stubs: Small colored bumps (mix of gray, blue, red) projecting outward from the helix at regular intervals, radiating away from the central axis. About 8-10 stubs visible.
  • Backbone: The orange-red ribbon IS the backbone — no separate backbone line needed

docs.title: Beta Pleated Sheet (right half of panel):
docs.text:
• Shape: 3-4 parallel flat arrows/ribbons running vertically, with a zigzag pleated appearance when viewed from the side
  • Arrow direction: Alternate arrows pointing up and down (antiparallel arrangement). Each arrow/ribbon is blue (#3498DB).
  • Pleating: The ribbons should have a visible zigzag or accordion-fold appearance — they are NOT flat. Show the pleating as gentle up-down waves along each strand.
  • Hydrogen bonds: Green dashed lines running horizontally between adjacent strands, connecting the pleated ridges. Show 5-6 green dashed lines between each pair of adjacent strands.
  • R-group stubs: Small colored bumps projecting above and below the plane of the sheet, alternating up/down along each strand. About 3-4 per strand.

Visual feel: Two clearly different secondary structures — one is a spiral coil, the other is a flat pleated arrangement. Both are stabilized by the same green hydrogen bonds.

docs.title: Panel 3 — Tertiary Structure
docs.text:
Draw a compact, globular folded protein filling most of the panel. This shows the entire polypeptide chain folded into its 3D shape.

  • Overall shape: An irregular, roughly spherical/globular mass — NOT a perfect sphere, but a lumpy, organic shape like a kidney or potato
  • Secondary structure elements visible inside:
  • 2-3 orange-red alpha helices (shown as coiled ribbon segments) embedded within the globular shape
  • 1-2 blue beta sheet regions (shown as flat arrow clusters) visible within the mass
  • Gray loops and coils connecting the helices and sheets
  • Interior (hydrophobic core): The center of the protein should be slightly darker/denser, showing that nonpolar amino acids (gray circles) cluster together away from water. Show 4-5 small gray circles packed in the interior.
  • Surface (hydrophilic exterior): The outside of the protein should show polar (blue) and charged (red, orange) amino acid bumps exposed to the water environment.
  • Disulfide bridges: 1-2 gold/yellow lines crossing through the protein interior, connecting two points on the surface. These should look like thick gold staples or bridges holding distant parts of the chain together.
  • Salt bridge: One pair of a red circle and an orange circle close together on the surface, with a small lightning-bolt or spark shape between them (no text — just a visual indicator of electrostatic attraction)
  • Hydrogen bonds between R-groups: 2-3 small green dashed lines visible on the surface between nearby amino acid bumps

Visual feel: A complex, folded 3D structure with visible elements of secondary structure inside. The emphasis is on COMPACT FOLDING with multiple types of stabilizing interactions.

docs.title: Panel 4 — Quaternary Structure (rightmost)
docs.text:
Draw a hemoglobin tetramer — four protein subunits assembled together into a functional complex.

  • Overall arrangement: Four globular subunits packed together symmetrically, like four lumpy balls nestled together in a 2×2 arrangement
  • Alpha subunits (×2): Light blue (#AED6F1) globular masses, positioned at upper-left and lower-right of the tetramer. Each should show faint coiled ribbon segments (alpha helices) within, similar to the tertiary panel but smaller and lighter.
  • Beta subunits (×2): Light pink/salmon (#F5B7B1) globular masses, positioned at upper-right and lower-left. Same internal structure hints as the alpha subunits.
  • Subunit interfaces: Where the four subunits touch, there should be visible contact surfaces — slight flattening where they press together, with a slightly darker line at the interface showing the boundary between subunits.
  • Heme groups: Inside each of the four subunits, one flat disk shape in dark red/maroon (#922B21). The disk should be oriented at a slight angle so it is clearly visible as a flat plate embedded within the globular subunit. Each disk is roughly 20% the diameter of its host subunit.
  • Oxygen molecules: 2-3 small bright red spheres (much smaller than the heme disks) sitting on top of or adjacent to the heme disks, representing O₂ binding. Not all four heme groups need to have oxygen bound — showing 2 with O₂ and 2 without suggests cooperative binding.

Visual feel: Multiple individual protein subunits (each resembling the tertiary structure) assembled into a larger functional machine. The emphasis is on MULTIPLE SUBUNITS WORKING TOGETHER.

docs.title: Composition Notes
docs.text:
• All four panels should be the same width
  • The structures should increase in visual complexity from left to right (simple linear chain → complex multi-subunit assembly)
  • Each structure should be centered vertically and horizontally within its panel
  • Leave enough white space around each structure for overlay labels (at least 10% padding on each side)
  • Color fills must be flat or with very subtle shading — no heavy gradients, no photorealistic rendering, no drop shadows
  • The style should be consistent across all four panels — same line weights, same level of detail, same artistic approach
  • Each panel's content should be roughly the same visual "weight" — don't make the primary structure tiny and the quaternary structure huge

No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image. This is critical — the interactive overlay adds all labels programmatically.

docs.title: DNA Replication Fork Explorer
docs.text: View Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text: This interactive diagram shows the complete enzymatic machinery at a DNA replication fork. Students can explore 13 labeled structures including helicase, DNA Polymerase III, primase, Okazaki fragments, DNA Polymerase I, and DNA ligase. Each callout provides a detailed description and an AP Exam Tip highlighting common misconceptions and exam strategies.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore Mode: Hover over any numbered marker or label to see a description of the structure, its function, and an AP exam tip.
  • Quiz Mode: Click the Quiz button to test your knowledge. Marker labels are hidden — click the correct marker when prompted to identify each structure. A gold star appears for each correct answer, and a celebration animation plays when you complete the quiz.

docs.title: Parental DNA Double Helix
docs.text: The original double-stranded DNA that serves as the template for replication. Each strand is used as a template to synthesize a new complementary strand (semiconservative replication).

docs.title: Topoisomerase
docs.text: Relieves torsional strain ahead of the replication fork by cutting, swiveling, and resealing DNA strands. Prevents supercoiling that would stall the fork.

docs.title: Helicase
docs.text: A ring-shaped enzyme that uses ATP energy to break hydrogen bonds between base pairs, unwinding the double helix at the fork junction.

docs.title: Single-Strand Binding Proteins (SSB)
docs.text: Coat exposed single-stranded DNA to prevent re-annealing and protect the template from nuclease degradation.

docs.title: RNA Primer
docs.text: A short RNA sequence synthesized by primase that provides the free 3'-OH group needed by DNA Polymerase III to begin synthesis. The leading strand requires only one primer; the lagging strand requires many.

docs.title: DNA Polymerase III
docs.text: The primary replication enzyme that synthesizes new DNA in the 5'→3' direction. It has proofreading ability (3'→5' exonuclease activity) with an error rate of about 1 in 10 billion base pairs.

docs.title: Leading Strand
docs.text: Synthesized continuously in the 5'→3' direction, following the movement of the replication fork. Requires only a single RNA primer.

docs.title: Lagging Strand and Okazaki Fragments
docs.text: Synthesized discontinuously as short fragments (Okazaki fragments), each 1,000–2,000 nucleotides long in prokaryotes. Each fragment requires its own RNA primer and is synthesized away from the fork.

docs.title: Primase
docs.text: An RNA polymerase that synthesizes RNA primers on the lagging strand template. Unlike DNA polymerase, primase can start new strands from scratch.

docs.title: DNA Polymerase I
docs.text: Removes RNA primers using 5'→3' exonuclease activity and replaces them with DNA nucleotides.

docs.title: DNA Ligase
docs.text: Seals the nicks between adjacent Okazaki fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds, creating a continuous sugar-phosphate backbone on the lagging strand.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: 9-12 (AP Biology)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• DNA structure (double helix, base pairing, antiparallel strands)
  • Enzyme function and specificity
  • 5'→3' directionality of nucleic acids

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Use Explore mode to examine each enzyme at the replication fork. Pay attention to the difference between leading and lagging strand synthesis.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Discuss with a partner why the lagging strand must be synthesized in fragments. Trace the 5'→3' direction on both strands.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Switch to Quiz mode and identify all 13 structures. Aim for a perfect score.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Identify all enzymes at the replication fork and state their functions
  • Explain why leading strand synthesis is continuous while lagging strand synthesis is discontinuous
  • Describe the roles of DNA Pol I and DNA Ligase in processing Okazaki fragments

DNA Replication Fork Explorer — Image Prompt

Overview
docs.text: Create a biological textbook illustration of a DNA replication fork viewed from above, showing the complete machinery of DNA replication. The image shows a Y-shaped replication fork with the parental double-stranded DNA on the left unwinding into two daughter strands on the right. All key enzymes and structural features must be clearly visible as distinct, color-coded shapes.

docs.title: Technical Specifications
docs.text:
• Aspect ratio: landscape 4:3
  • Resolution: 1200 × 900 px
  • Style: biological textbook illustration, clean line art with light color fills, white background, AP Biology high school level
  • Background: clean white, no gradients or artistic flourishes

docs.title: CRITICAL: No text, labels, numbers, arrows, callout lines, leader lines, or annotation marks anywhere in the image.
Spatial Layout
docs.text:
The fork opens from left to right:

  • Left side (left quarter): Intact double-stranded parental DNA helix, shown as two intertwined strands (medium gray #888888 and light gray #AAAAAA) with visible base-pair rungs. A small round protein (topoisomerase, gold #DAA520) sits ahead of the fork on the unreplicated DNA.
  • Center (fork junction): A large ring-shaped enzyme (helicase, bright blue #2196F3) sits at the junction point where the two strands separate. The helicase is wedge-shaped or donut-shaped, clearly splitting the two strands apart.
  • Upper right (leading strand, top half): The template strand runs 3'→5' from the fork toward the upper right. A large oval enzyme (DNA Polymerase III, forest green #2E7D32) sits on this strand, synthesizing a new complementary strand (bright green #4CAF50) continuously. A short red segment (RNA primer, red #F44336) is visible at the very start of the new strand near the fork. Small oval proteins (SSB proteins, teal #009688) coat the single-stranded template between helicase and Pol III.
  • Lower right (lagging strand, bottom half): The template strand runs 5'→3' from the fork toward the lower right. Multiple short segments of new DNA (Okazaki fragments, royal blue #1565C0) are visible, each preceded by a short red RNA primer segment (#F44336). A DNA Pol III enzyme (forest green #2E7D32, same color as leading strand Pol III) sits on the most recently started fragment nearest the fork. A smaller oval enzyme (primase, orange #FF9800) is shown laying down a new primer ahead of the newest fragment. Further from the fork, a medium-sized enzyme (DNA Polymerase I, purple #7B1FA2) is shown removing a primer from an older fragment. Between two completed fragments, a small enzyme (DNA Ligase, hot pink #E91E63) is shown sealing the nick where fragments join.

docs.title: Structure Details (each must have clear landing zone ≥30 px)
docs.text:
• Parental DNA double helix — two intertwined strands in medium gray (#888888) and light gray (#AAAAAA) with horizontal base-pair rungs between them; occupies the left quarter of the image. Must show clear helical twist.

  • Topoisomerase — small, round, gold (#DAA520) protein sitting on the parental DNA ahead of (left of) the fork junction. Appears to grip both strands of the helix.

  • Helicase — large, ring-shaped or wedge-shaped enzyme in bright blue (#2196F3) at the fork junction. Clearly positioned at the point where the two parental strands separate. This is the most prominent enzyme at the fork center.

  • Single-strand binding proteins (SSB) — multiple small oval/bean shapes in teal (#009688) coating the single-stranded regions of both template strands between the helicase and the polymerases. Show at least 4-5 SSB proteins clustered along each exposed strand.

  • Leading strand template — the upper template strand running from the fork toward upper right, in medium gray (#888888). Single-stranded where exposed.

  • New leading strand — continuous new strand in bright green (#4CAF50) complementary to the leading template, synthesized from the fork rightward. Runs parallel to the template.

  • DNA Polymerase III (leading) — large oval enzyme in forest green (#2E7D32) sitting at the growing tip of the new leading strand (upper right area). Clearly larger than SSB proteins.

  • RNA primer (leading strand) — a short red (#F44336) segment at the 5' start of the new leading strand, near the fork origin. Clearly different color from the green new strand.

  • Lagging strand template — the lower template strand running from the fork toward lower right, in light gray (#AAAAAA). Single-stranded where exposed.

  • Okazaki fragments — 3-4 short segments of new DNA in royal blue (#1565C0) on the lagging strand, each about 1/6 the length of the leading strand. They are synthesized in the direction AWAY from the fork (toward the left).

  • RNA primers (lagging strand) — short red (#F44336) segments at the 5' end of each Okazaki fragment. At least 3 visible primers.

  • Primase — small oval enzyme in orange (#FF9800) on the lagging template strand near the fork, shown laying down a new RNA primer. Distinct from the larger Pol III.

  • DNA Polymerase III (lagging) — large oval enzyme in forest green (#2E7D32) on the lagging strand, extending the most recent Okazaki fragment nearest the fork.

  • DNA Polymerase I — medium oval enzyme in purple (#7B1FA2) on the lagging strand further from the fork, positioned where it is removing/replacing an RNA primer with DNA.

  • DNA Ligase — small enzyme in hot pink (#E91E63) positioned at a nick between two completed Okazaki fragments, shown sealing the gap.

docs.title: Structural Connections
docs.text:
• The helicase must be visually splitting the parental strands at the fork junction
  • SSB proteins must be touching the single-stranded DNA regions
  • Each Pol III must be clearly associated with its respective strand
  • Okazaki fragments must show gaps/nicks between them
  • Primase must be on the lagging strand template, near the fork
  • DNA Pol I must be near an older Okazaki fragment, associated with a primer being removed
  • DNA Ligase must be between two adjacent Okazaki fragments

Overview
docs.text: The scientific method is the systematic process that scientists use to investigate phenomena, acquire new knowledge, and correct or integrate existing knowledge. This interactive flowchart visualizes each step of the scientific method as used in physics and all scientific disciplines.

docs.title: Interactive Diagram
docs.text:
View Fullscreen

<iframe src="main.html" width="100%" height="1600px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Process Steps
docs.text:
1. Observe Phenomenon or Ask Question - Notice something interesting about the physical world—like why objects fall, why the sky is blue, or how magnets work
  2. Background Research - Review existing scientific literature and previous experiments to understand what's already known
  3. Formulate Hypothesis - Create a testable statement predicting the relationship between variables (e.g., "If mass increases, then falling time decreases")
  4. Design Experiment - Plan controlled procedures, identify independent and dependent variables, consider controls and constants
  5. Conduct Experiment & Collect Data - Carefully follow procedures, make accurate measurements, record all observations systematically
  6. Analyze Data - Create graphs, calculate statistics, look for patterns and relationships in the measurements
  7. Does Data Support Hypothesis? - Compare experimental results to predictions—do they match within experimental error?
  8. Accept Hypothesis (if Yes) - Hypothesis is supported by evidence, but remains open to future testing and refinement
  9. Revise or Reject Hypothesis (if No) - Modify hypothesis based on findings or develop an entirely new hypothesis
  10. Communicate Results - Share findings through lab reports, presentations, or scientific papers using standard formats
  11. New Questions Raised? - Scientific investigation often leads to new questions and avenues for research

docs.title: Understanding the Process
docs.text: The scientific method is not a rigid linear process but rather a flexible, iterative approach to investigation. The flowchart illustrates several key features:

docs.title: Core Steps
docs.text:
1. Observation & Question - Scientific inquiry begins with curiosity about the natural world. In physics, this might involve noticing patterns in motion, energy, or forces.

  2. Background Research - Before conducting experiments, scientists review existing knowledge to understand what has already been discovered and to refine their questions.

  3. Hypothesis Formation - A hypothesis is a testable prediction about the relationship between variables. In physics, hypotheses often take the form of mathematical relationships (e.g., "acceleration is inversely proportional to mass").

  4. Experimental Design - Careful planning identifies independent variables (what you change), dependent variables (what you measure), and controlled variables (what you keep constant).

  5. Data Collection - Systematic observation and measurement following established procedures. Accuracy, precision, and reproducibility are essential.

  6. Data Analysis - Raw data is processed using graphs, statistical analysis, and mathematical models to identify patterns and relationships.

docs.title: Decision Points
docs.text:
The diagram includes two critical decision points:

  • Does Data Support Hypothesis? - If experimental results match predictions within acceptable error margins, the hypothesis is supported. If not, it must be revised or rejected.

  • New Questions Raised? - Scientific investigation typically generates new questions, leading to additional cycles of inquiry.

docs.title: The Iterative Nature
docs.text: Notice the feedback loops in the diagram: - Failed hypotheses loop back to reformulation based on experimental evidence - Successful investigations often reveal new questions, restarting the cycle - Each iteration builds on previous knowledge, advancing scientific understanding

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
• Controlled Experiment: An investigation where one variable is changed while others are held constant
  • Independent Variable: The factor deliberately manipulated by the experimenter
  • Dependent Variable: The factor measured in response to changes in the independent variable
  • Hypothesis: A testable prediction about the relationship between variables
  • Reproducibility: The ability of an experiment to yield consistent results when repeated
  • Peer Review: The process of scientists evaluating each other's work before publication

docs.title: Connection to Physics Learning
docs.text:
Throughout this course, you will apply the scientific method to explore:

  • Kinematics: Investigating relationships between position, velocity, and acceleration
  • Dynamics: Testing Newton's laws through force and motion experiments
  • Energy: Analyzing energy transformations and conservation principles
  • Waves & Optics: Examining wave behaviors and light phenomena

Each physics concept in this textbook was discovered and refined through countless iterations of this process.

docs.text: These links do not exist! - [Experimental Error and Uncertainty](../../chapters/01/index.md) - Understanding measurement limitations - [Graphing and Data Analysis](../../chapters/01/index.md) - Visualizing experimental results - [Significant Figures](../../chapters/01/index.md) - Reporting measurements accurately

docs.title: Further Exploration
docs.text:
Try applying the scientific method to these physics questions:

  1. Does the angle of a ramp affect how fast an object slides down?
  2. How does the length of a pendulum affect its period?
  3. What factors influence the range of a projectile?

For each question, work through the flowchart: formulate a hypothesis, design an experiment, and predict what data analysis might show.

docs.title: Classes of Diagram Architectures for Overlay MicroSims
Classes of Diagram Architectures for Overlay MicroSims
docs.text:
The user has been very happy with the quality if detailed images created with text-to-image models. Our goal is to centralize these algorithms in the @docs/sims/shared-libs directory. A draft diagram.js file is located there.

There are currently four different types of Diagram Overlay MicroSims. All of these use the pattern of using a text-to-image LLM to generate an image. The difference is how complex the overlay javascript must be. In all of these examples, the names and boundaries of each of the regions are stored in a overlay.json overlay file within the MicroSim directory. The diagram.js program fires the correct event for each region. Adding the edit=true parameter allows the user to edit the regions.

Here are some examples:

  1. Type 1: Simple non-overlapping rectangles - this is when the underlying image has regular rectangles that the user will hover over an click on. This is ideal for vertical or horizontal panels or a regular array of regions (2x3, 3X2, 3X3 etc) When the user hovers or clicks within a rectangle, an appropriate event occurs. The edit mode allows the user to change the edges and corners of the rectangles.
  2. Type 2: Complex Polygons - this is when the underlying image can not be decomposed into non-overlapping rectangles. In this example polygons with three to many edges must be stored in the overlay.json overlay file. The diagram.js fires the correct event for each region the the user is hovering over or clicking on. The edit mode allows the user to move the existing points in the polygon, remove an edge point or add a new edge point.
  3. Type 3: Callout Points to Edge Regions - in this mode, different regions of the image have points that also have lines to the edges of the diagram where the labels of the points give the name of the point. The user can go into edit mode and move the points around the drawing and also reorder the labels around the edges. The user can place a checkbox in the control region called "Show Numbers" that will toggle numbers at the callout points. The default is "Show Numbers" on.
  4. Type 4: Callout Points to Floating Labels - in this mode, the user can have a callout line to a label that is placed anywhere in the diagram. In the edit mode, the user can change the location of the callout points and the location of the labels by dragging them anywhere over the diagram.

Currently we only have Type 1 and Type 3 working.

docs.title: Layout Modes
docs.text:
The shared diagram.js supports three layout modes, set via "layout" in data.json:

  1. side-panel (default) — Image left (65%), labels right (35%). Best for single-subject diagrams (e.g., animal cell, neuron).
  2. top-bottom — Label strips above and below the image. Best for horizontal cross-sections (e.g., cell membrane). Each callout gets "panel": "top" or "panel": "bottom".
  3. dual-panel — Labels left (22%) | image center (56%) | labels right (22%). Best for comparison diagrams where structures belong to two groups (e.g., prokaryote vs. eukaryote). Each callout gets "panel": "left" or "panel": "right".

All diagrams can also have a quiz mode which shows a gold star for each correct answer and a celebration animation for completing a quiz.

docs.title: Diagram Title (Required)
docs.text:
Every diagram overlay main.html must include a visible title at the top center of the page, above the Explore/Quiz controls:

<h2 id="diagram-title">DNA Replication Fork</h2>

Style it with a small inline <style> block:

#diagram-title {
  text-align: center;
  font-size: 1.4rem;
  margin: 4px 0 2px;
  color: #1a1a1a;
}

The title should be a short, descriptive name for the diagram — not the full MicroSim title (omit "Explorer", "Interactive Diagram", etc.).

For dual-panel layouts where the two panels represent distinct biological subjects (e.g., prokaryote vs. eukaryote), add <h3> region labels above each panel. Omit region labels when the panels are just a spatial convenience for distributing callouts.

docs.title: Initial Marker Placement
docs.text:
When creating a new data.json, never stack all callout markers at the same coordinate (e.g., x: 50, y: 50). Stacked markers are impossible to distinguish or drag individually in edit mode.

Instead, spread initial y values evenly from top to bottom at x = 50: - Range: y ≈ 7 to y ≈ 93 - Step: 86 / (N - 1) where N is the number of callouts - Example with 13 callouts: y = 7, 14, 21, 29, 36, 43, 50, 57, 64, 71, 79, 86, 93

This makes every marker individually visible and draggable on first load in edit mode, before the image has been calibrated.

docs.title: Signal Transduction Pathway Overview
docs.text: View Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text: This interactive diagram illustrates the complete signal transduction pathway from ligand binding at a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) through the cAMP second messenger cascade to cellular responses including enzyme activation and gene expression changes. Students can explore 13 labeled structures across the three stages of cell signaling: reception, transduction, and response.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore mode: Hover over any numbered marker or label to learn about that structure. The infobox below shows a detailed description and AP Exam tips for each component.
  • Quiz mode: Click the Quiz button to test your knowledge. Markers show "?" and you must click the correct structure when prompted.
  • Edit mode: Add ?edit=true to the URL to calibrate marker positions on the image.

docs.title: Reception Stage
docs.text:
1. Signal molecule (ligand) — The first messenger; binds specifically to the GPCR extracellular domain
  2. GPCR (receptor) — Seven-transmembrane receptor that undergoes conformational change upon ligand binding
  3. Cell membrane — Phospholipid bilayer barrier that prevents hydrophilic signals from entering the cell

docs.title: Transduction Stage
docs.text:
1. G-protein (inactive) — Heterotrimeric protein (Gα-GDP + Gβγ) docked on the membrane's intracellular face
  2. Active Gα-GTP subunit — Dissociated alpha subunit that activates adenylyl cyclase
  3. Adenylyl cyclase — Membrane-embedded enzyme that converts ATP to cAMP
  4. cAMP (second messenger) — Small diffusible molecule that activates PKA
  5. PKA (protein kinase A) — Enzyme that phosphorylates downstream targets
  6. Phosphorylation cascade — Sequential kinase activation providing exponential signal amplification

docs.title: Response Stage
docs.text:
1. Target enzyme (activated) — Final effector enzyme producing the cellular response
  2. Nucleus — Site of gene expression changes triggered by the signaling pathway
  3. Transcription factors — Proteins activated by phosphorylation that enter the nucleus to regulate gene expression
  4. Gene expression (cellular response) — Transcription of specific genes into mRNA, producing lasting cellular changes

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: 9-12 (AP Biology)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Cell membrane structure and selective permeability
  • Protein structure and enzyme function
  • Basic understanding of ATP and phosphorylation

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Use Explore mode to trace the pathway from ligand to cellular response. Identify where amplification occurs at each step.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Discuss how the same ligand (epinephrine) can produce different responses in different cell types through the same GPCR-cAMP pathway.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Use Quiz mode to identify all 13 structures. Aim for a perfect score!

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Students can name and describe the function of each pathway component
  • Students can explain signal amplification at the G-protein, adenylyl cyclase, and kinase cascade steps
  • Students can distinguish between fast responses (enzyme activation) and slow responses (gene expression)
